title: Consolidated text: Regulation(EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Councilof 13 June 2024
summary: This text is a documentation version of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act, adopted by the European Parliament and Council on 13 June 2024, amending multiple existing EU regulations and directives. It notes amendment by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and includes a disclaimer that only Official Journal versions have legal effect. Chapter I covers General Provisions. Article 1 outlines the Regulation's purpose: improving internal market functioning, promoting human-centric trustworthy AI, protecting health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environment, while supporting innovation. It establishes harmonised rules for AI systems' marketing and use, prohibits certain AI practices, sets requirements for high-risk AI systems, transparency rules, rules for general-purpose AI models, market surveillance and governance, and innovation support for SMEs and SMCs. Article 2 defines scope, applying to providers (regardless of location) placing AI systems or general-purpose AI models in the Union, and deployers established within the Union.

nodes.title: CHAPTER I GENERAL PROVISIONS
Article 1 Subject matter'
nodes.summary: This text is the opening portion of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and Council, dated 13 June 2024, known as the Artificial Intelligence Act. It establishes harmonised AI rules and amends several existing regulations and directives. Chapter I covers General Provisions. Article 1 outlines the subject matter: improving the internal market, promoting human-centric and trustworthy AI, protecting health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and the environment, while supporting innovation. The Regulation sets out: harmonised rules for placing AI systems on the market and into service; prohibitions of certain AI practices; requirements for high-risk AI systems and operator obligations; transparency rules; rules for general-purpose AI models; market monitoring, surveillance, governance and enforcement; and innovation support measures focused on SMCs, SMEs, and start-ups. Article 2 defines scope, applying to providers (regardless of location) placing AI systems or general-purpose AI models in the Union, and to deployers established or located within the Union.

nodes.title: Article 2 Scope
nodes.summary: This text presents the opening sections of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation 2024/1689), adopted 13 June 2024. Chapter I covers General Provisions. Article 1 (Subject matter) states the regulation's purpose: improving internal market functioning, promoting trustworthy human-centric AI, protecting health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environment, while supporting innovation. It lays down harmonised rules on AI system placement/use, prohibits certain practices, sets high-risk AI requirements, transparency rules, general-purpose AI model rules, governance/enforcement rules, and innovation support for SMEs/SMCs/startups. Article 2 (Scope) identifies who it applies to (providers, deployers, importers, distributors, manufacturers, representatives, affected persons) and exclusions including national security, military/defence uses, third-country law enforcement cooperation, scientific R&D, pre-market testing, personal non-professional use, and free/open-source AI (with exceptions). It preserves data protection laws and worker protections. Article 3 provides definitions including AI system, risk, provider, deployer, authorised representative, importer, distributor, operator, placing on the market, making available, and putting into service.

nodes.title: Article 3 Definitions
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) contains Article 3, which provides 68 definitions of key terms used throughout the regulation. These include foundational concepts such as 'AI system,' 'risk,' 'provider,' 'deployer,' 'authorised representative,' 'importer,' 'distributor,' and 'operator'; market-related terms like 'placing on the market,' 'making available,' and 'putting into service'; product-related terms including 'intended purpose,' 'reasonably foreseeable misuse,' 'safety component,' and 'substantial modification'; enterprise classifications (SME, SMC); compliance terms such as 'conformity assessment,' 'notified body,' 'CE marking,' 'harmonised standard,' and 'post-market monitoring'; data categories (training, validation, testing, input, biometric, personal, sensitive); biometric and recognition systems; law enforcement definitions; governance terms (AI Office, national competent authority, serious incident); sandbox and real-world testing concepts; 'deep fake,' 'critical infrastructure,' 'widespread infringement'; and general-purpose AI model terminology including 'systemic risk,' 'high-impact capabilities,' and 'downstream provider.' It also includes Article 4 on AI literacy, requiring providers and deployers to ensure staff competence, supported by the Commission and Member States.

nodes.title: Article 4 AI literacy
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) contains two main sections. First, it provides definitions (items 63-68) for key terms: 'general-purpose AI model', 'high-impact capabilities', 'systemic risk', 'general-purpose AI system', 'floating-point operation', and 'downstream provider'. Second, it presents Article 4 on AI literacy, requiring providers and deployers to ensure staff AI literacy considering technical knowledge and context, with Commission and Member State support (especially for SMEs) and Board recommendations based on European competence frameworks. Article 4a addresses processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction in high-risk AI systems, allowing exceptional processing under strict conditions: necessity (no alternative data works), technical limitations, security measures including pseudonymisation, access controls, no transmission to third parties, deletion after correction, and documentation requirements. Paragraph 2 extends these provisions to providers/deployers of other AI systems where bias could affect health, safety, fundamental rights, or cause discrimination.

nodes.title: Article 4a Processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers two main areas. First, it addresses AI literacy, requiring the Board to adopt recommendations supporting the Commission and Member States. Article 4a permits providers of high-risk AI systems to exceptionally process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, subject to conditions: no alternative data suffices, technical limitations and security measures (including pseudonymisation), restricted access, no third-party transmission, deletion after correction/retention, and documented justification. Providers/deployers of other AI systems may do so when necessary to prevent biases affecting health, safety, fundamental rights, or discrimination, without creating an obligation. Second, Chapter II Article 5 lists prohibited AI practices: subliminal/manipulative/deceptive techniques causing harm; exploitation of vulnerabilities (age, disability, socio-economic); non-consensual generation/manipulation of intimate or sexually explicit imagery of identifiable persons; generation of child sexual abuse material per Directive 2011/93/EU; and social scoring leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts.

Chapter I of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), adopted 13 June 2024, sets out general provisions. Article 1 defines the subject matter: harmonising AI rules to improve the internal market, promote trustworthy human-centric AI, protect health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and the environment, while supporting innovation. It covers prohibitions, high-risk AI requirements, transparency, general-purpose AI models, governance, enforcement, and innovation support for SMEs/SMCs/startups. Article 2 defines scope and actors covered (providers, deployers, importers, distributors, etc.) and exclusions (national security, military, R&D, personal use, open-source with exceptions), preserving data protection and worker rights. Article 3 provides 68 definitions covering AI systems, operators, market placement, products, enterprises, compliance, data, biometrics, law enforcement, governance, sandboxes, deepfakes, and general-purpose AI terminology. Article 4 mandates AI literacy for staff. Article 4a permits exceptional processing of special personal data categories for bias detection/correction under strict conditions.

nodes.title: CHAPTER II PROHIBITED AI PRACTICES
key_items: 1. The following AI practices shall be prohibited:
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), Chapter II Article 5, lists prohibited AI practices, including: subliminal/manipulative techniques causing harm; exploitation of vulnerabilities; non-consensual generation of intimate/sexual imagery; generation of child sexual abuse material; social scoring; predictive policing based solely on profiling; untargeted scraping for facial recognition databases; emotion inference in workplaces/schools; biometric categorisation inferring sensitive traits; and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement (with narrow exceptions for victim searches, imminent threats, or serious crimes). It specifies conditions for prohibitions on AI-generated intimate content, and details safeguards for biometric identification use: necessity/proportionality assessments, prior judicial authorisation, fundamental rights impact assessments, EU database registration, notifications to authorities, annual reporting by Member States and the Commission, and national law provisions. Chapter III Article 6 begins classification rules for high-risk AI systems based on safety-component status under Union harmonisation legislation, clarifying what qualifies as safety components.

nodes.title: CHAPTER III HIGH-RISK AI SYSTEMS
SECTION 1 Classification of AI systems as high-risk
key_items: Article 6 Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers reporting obligations and high-risk AI system classification. Article 5(6-8) requires national market surveillance and data protection authorities to submit annual reports to the Commission on real-time remote biometric identification use for law enforcement, with the Commission publishing aggregated annual reports excluding sensitive operational data. Chapter III, Section 1 addresses high-risk AI classification: Article 6 defines systems as high-risk when used as safety components under Annex I harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, with M1 amendments clarifying that non-safety-related functions don't qualify as safety components, but malfunctioning systems endangering health/safety do. Annex III systems are high-risk unless they pose no significant risk (narrow procedural tasks, improving human results, pattern detection, preparatory tasks), though profiling always qualifies. Providers must document assessments. Article 7 empowers the Commission to amend Annex III via delegated acts based on specified risk criteria. Article 8 mandates compliance with Section 2 requirements.

nodes.title: SECTION 2 Requirements for high-risk AI systems
Article 8 Compliance with the requirements
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) outlines criteria for assessing high-risk AI systems. It lists factors including: potential extent/intensity of harm, dependence on AI outcomes, power imbalances or vulnerability of affected persons, reversibility of outcomes, benefits of deployment, and existing Union law protections. It empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts removing AI systems from Annex III when they no longer pose significant risks and removal doesn't reduce protection levels. Section 2 (Article 8) requires high-risk AI systems to comply with requirements considering intended purpose and state of the art, allowing integration with existing Union harmonisation legislation procedures. Article 9 mandates a risk management system as a continuous iterative lifecycle process involving: identifying foreseeable risks to health/safety/fundamental rights, estimating risks under intended use and foreseeable misuse, evaluating post-market monitoring data, and adopting targeted mitigation measures. Residual risks must be judged acceptable, with measures balanced across combined requirements.

nodes.title: Article 9 Risk management system
nodes.summary: This excerpt from Regulation 2024/1689 covers compliance and risk management requirements for high-risk AI systems. It states that providers of products containing AI systems must ensure full compliance with applicable Union harmonisation legislation, allowing integration of testing, reporting, and documentation processes with existing procedures to avoid duplication. Article 9 mandates establishing a continuous, iterative risk management system throughout the AI system's lifecycle, including: identifying foreseeable risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights; estimating risks under intended use and foreseeable misuse; evaluating post-market monitoring data; and adopting targeted mitigation measures. Residual risks must be acceptable, achieved through design, mitigation controls, and deployer information/training. Testing must verify consistent performance against predefined metrics before market placement and may include real-world testing. Providers must consider impacts on minors and vulnerable groups. Requirements may be combined with existing risk management obligations under other EU law. Article 10 begins addressing data governance, requiring quality training, validation, and testing datasets.

nodes.title: Article 10 Data and data governance
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers requirements for high-risk AI systems. It outlines risk management measures including elimination/reduction of risks through design, mitigation controls, and user information/training, with consideration of deployer knowledge and usage context. It mandates testing against predefined metrics throughout development, possibly in real-world conditions, with special attention to impacts on minors and vulnerable groups. Article 10 addresses data governance, requiring quality training/validation/testing datasets with proper practices covering design choices, data collection, preparation, bias examination/mitigation, and gap identification; datasets must be relevant, representative, error-free, and account for geographical/contextual specifics. Article 11 requires technical documentation (per Annex IV) before market placement, with simplified forms available for SMEs and startups, and empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts. Article 12 mandates automatic event logging (traceability) over the system's lifetime to identify risks, facilitate post-market monitoring, and track operations.

nodes.title: Article 11 Technical documentation
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers two articles on high-risk AI systems. Article 11 (Technical Documentation) requires technical documentation to be prepared before market placement and kept updated, demonstrating compliance with regulatory requirements and containing elements listed in Annex IV. SMEs, start-ups, and SMCs may use a simplified form established by the Commission, which notified bodies must accept. For AI systems tied to products under Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I, Section A), a single integrated documentation set is required. The Commission may adopt delegated acts to amend Annex IV in light of technical progress. Article 12 (Record-keeping) mandates that high-risk AI systems technically allow automatic event logging throughout their lifetime, ensuring traceability appropriate to intended purpose. Logging must enable identifying risk situations or substantial modifications (per Article 79(1)), facilitating post-market monitoring (Article 72), and monitoring operations of systems referenced in Article 26(5).

nodes.title: Article 12 Record-keeping
nodes.summary: This text chunk from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers Articles 11-13 on high-risk AI systems. Article 11 (Technical documentation) requires documentation be drawn up before market placement, kept updated, demonstrate compliance per Annex IV, with simplified forms available for SMEs/startups/SMCs; single documentation sets apply when products fall under Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I Section A); the Commission may adopt delegated acts to amend Annex IV. Article 12 (Record-keeping) mandates automatic event logging over the system's lifetime to ensure traceability, identify risks, facilitate post-market monitoring, and monitor operations; for Annex III point 1(a) systems, logs must record usage periods, reference databases, matched input data, and persons verifying results. Article 13 (Transparency) requires high-risk AI systems to be transparent enough for deployers to interpret outputs, accompanied by clear instructions for use including provider identity/contacts, system characteristics, intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity metrics, foreseeable risks to health/safety/fundamental rights, and explanation capabilities.

nodes.title: Article 13 Transparency and provision of information to deployers
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers provisions on high-risk AI systems. It specifies minimum logging requirements for systems in Annex III point 1(a), including recording usage periods, reference databases, matched input data, and persons verifying results. Article 13 mandates transparency and information provision to deployers, requiring systems to be designed for interpretability and accompanied by clear instructions for use. These instructions must include provider identity/contact, system characteristics (intended purpose, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, foreseeable risks to health/safety/fundamental rights, explainability features, performance on specific groups, input data specifications, output interpretation), pre-determined changes, human oversight measures, computational/hardware needs, lifetime, maintenance, and log collection mechanisms. Article 14 requires human oversight through appropriate human-machine interfaces to prevent risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights. Oversight measures must be proportionate to risks, autonomy, and context, implemented either by the provider pre-market or by the deployer.

nodes.title: Article 14 Human oversight
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers requirements for high-risk AI systems. It details information providers must supply, including system performance for specific persons/groups, input data specifications, output interpretation guidance, pre-determined changes, human oversight measures, computational/hardware resources, lifetime, maintenance needs, and log collection mechanisms. Article 14 mandates human oversight to minimize health, safety, and fundamental rights risks, requiring measures proportionate to risk and autonomy, built-in by providers or implemented by deployers. Oversight personnel must understand system capabilities, be aware of automation bias, interpret outputs correctly, decide not to use or override outputs, and intervene via stop mechanisms. For biometric identification systems (Annex III point 1(a)), two-person verification is required, with exceptions for law enforcement, migration, border control, or asylum where disproportionate. Article 15 requires appropriate accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity throughout the lifecycle, with the Commission encouraging benchmark development, and accuracy levels declared in instructions.

nodes.title: Article 15 Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers requirements for high-risk AI systems. Article 14 (continued) outlines human oversight provisions, enabling overseers to understand system capacities, avoid automation bias, interpret outputs, decide not to use the system, and intervene via stop mechanisms. For biometric identification systems (Annex III, point 1(a)), identifications must be verified by at least two competent persons, with exceptions for law enforcement, migration, border control, and asylum where disproportionate. Article 15 addresses accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, requiring consistent lifecycle performance, Commission-encouraged benchmarks, declared accuracy metrics in instructions, resilience to errors through technical redundancy and fail-safe plans, mitigation of feedback loops in continuously learning systems, and protection against attacks including data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, and confidentiality attacks. Article 16 begins listing provider obligations: ensuring compliance, identification labeling, maintaining a quality management system, keeping documentation, and preserving automatically generated logs.

Section 2 of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) establishes requirements for high-risk AI systems across Articles 8-15. Article 8 requires compliance considering intended purpose and state of the art, allowing integration with existing Union harmonisation legislation to avoid duplication. Article 9 mandates a continuous, iterative risk management system throughout the lifecycle, covering risk identification, estimation, evaluation of post-market data, and targeted mitigation, with special attention to minors and vulnerable groups. Article 10 requires quality data governance for training, validation, and testing datasets, ensuring relevance, representativeness, and bias mitigation. Article 11 mandates technical documentation per Annex IV, with simplified forms for SMEs/startups. Article 12 requires automatic event logging for traceability. Article 13 ensures transparency through clear instructions covering system characteristics, risks, and operation. Article 14 requires human oversight measures, including two-person verification for biometric identification systems. Article 15 mandates accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, including protection against data/model poisoning and adversarial attacks.

nodes.title: SECTION 3 Obligations of providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems and other parties
Article 16 Obligations of providers of high-risk AI systems
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers requirements and obligations for high-risk AI systems. Paragraph 4 mandates resilience against errors, faults, and inconsistencies through technical/organizational measures, redundancy, fail-safes, and mitigation of feedback loops in continuously learning systems. Paragraph 5 requires cybersecurity resilience against unauthorized third-party attacks, addressing AI-specific vulnerabilities like data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks, and model flaws. Section 3, Article 16 lists providers' obligations: ensuring compliance, identification labeling, maintaining a quality management system, documentation, log-keeping, conformity assessment, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, registration, corrective actions, demonstrating conformity to authorities, and meeting accessibility requirements per Directives 2016/2102 and 2019/882. Article 17 details the quality management system requirements, including documented written policies covering regulatory compliance strategy, design control/verification techniques, development and quality assurance procedures, examination/test/validation procedures with their frequency, and technical specifications/standards to be applied.

nodes.title: Article 17 Quality management system
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 outlines provider obligations for high-risk AI systems. It lists requirements including conformity assessment, drawing up EU declarations of conformity, affixing CE marking, registration, corrective actions, demonstrating conformity upon request, and ensuring accessibility compliance with Directives 2016/2102 and 2019/882. Article 17 mandates a documented quality management system covering: regulatory compliance strategy, design and development procedures, testing and validation, technical specifications, data management, risk management, post-market monitoring, serious incident reporting, communication with authorities, record-keeping, resource management, and an accountability framework. Implementation must be proportionate to organisation size (notably SMEs/start-ups/SMCs). Providers already subject to sectoral Union law may integrate these aspects into existing systems. Financial institutions complying with Union financial services law on internal governance are deemed compliant, except for points (g), (h), (i). Article 18 begins, requiring providers to keep documentation available to authorities for 10 years after market placement.

nodes.title: Article 18 Documentation keeping
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 outlines obligations for providers of high-risk AI systems. It continues listing required elements of a quality management system (Article 17), including data management procedures, risk management, post-market monitoring, serious incident reporting, communication with authorities, record-keeping, resource management, and accountability frameworks. Implementation must be proportionate to organization size (especially for SMEs), and financial institutions may integrate these within existing governance frameworks. Article 18 requires providers to retain technical documentation, quality management records, notified body decisions, and EU declarations of conformity for 10 years, with Member States determining conditions in cases of bankruptcy. Article 19 mandates keeping automatically generated logs for at least six months. Article 20 requires providers to take immediate corrective actions (withdrawal, disabling, recall) when a high-risk AI system is non-compliant and to inform distributors, deployers, authorised representatives, and importers.

nodes.title: Article 19 Automatically generated logs
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) outlines obligations for providers of high-risk AI systems. It lists required documentation to be kept available for national authorities, including technical documentation, quality management system records, notified body approvals and decisions, and the EU declaration of conformity. Member States must set conditions ensuring documentation remains accessible if providers go bankrupt or cease activity. Financial institution providers may integrate this documentation with records kept under Union financial services law. Article 19 requires providers to retain automatically generated logs from high-risk AI systems for at least six months, with similar integration allowances for financial institutions. Article 20 mandates that providers who suspect non-conformity of a high-risk AI system must immediately take corrective actions—bringing it into conformity, withdrawing, disabling, or recalling it—and inform distributors, deployers, authorised representatives, and importers accordingly.

nodes.title: Article 20 Corrective actions and duty of information
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) outlines obligations for providers of high-risk AI systems. It specifies documentation requirements including technical documentation, quality management system records, notified body decisions, and EU declarations of conformity, with provisions for provider bankruptcy and financial institutions. Article 19 requires providers to retain automatically generated logs for at least six months. Article 20 mandates immediate corrective actions (withdrawal, disabling, recall) for non-conforming systems and notification of distributors, deployers, authorities, and notified bodies when risks arise. Article 21 requires cooperation with competent authorities, providing information, documentation, and log access in accessible EU languages, subject to confidentiality under Article 78. Article 22 requires providers established in third countries to appoint an authorised representative in the Union via written mandate, who must verify the EU declaration of conformity and technical documentation and provide the mandate to market surveillance authorities upon request.

nodes.title: Article 21 Cooperation with competent authorities
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers obligations for providers of high-risk AI systems. It requires providers aware of risks under Article 79(1) to investigate causes with deployers and inform market surveillance authorities and notified bodies about non-compliance and corrective actions. Article 21 mandates cooperation with competent authorities: providers must supply information and documentation demonstrating conformity in an accessible EU language, grant access to automatically generated logs under their control, with all information treated confidentially per Article 78. Article 22 requires providers established in third countries to appoint, by written mandate, an authorised representative established in the Union before placing systems on the market. The representative must perform mandated tasks, provide the mandate copy to market surveillance authorities upon request, and verify that the EU declaration of conformity, technical documentation, and appropriate conformity assessment procedures have been completed by the provider.

nodes.title: Article 22 Authorised representatives of providers of high-risk AI systems
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers obligations related to high-risk AI systems. It mandates providers to investigate risks, inform market surveillance authorities and notified bodies of non-compliance and corrective actions. Article 21 requires providers to cooperate with competent authorities by providing necessary documentation, information, and access to automatically generated logs in an understandable EU language, with confidentiality safeguards. Article 22 obligates third-country providers to appoint an EU-established authorised representative via written mandate, who must verify conformity documentation, retain records for 10 years, supply information to authorities, cooperate on risk mitigation, and handle registration obligations. The representative must terminate the mandate if the provider breaches obligations and notify authorities. Article 23 outlines importer duties: before placing high-risk AI systems on the market, importers must verify that conformity assessment was performed, technical documentation prepared, CE marking and EU declaration of conformity present, and an authorised representative appointed.

nodes.title: Article 23 Obligations of importers
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) details obligations for authorised representatives, importers, and distributors of high-risk AI systems. Authorised representatives must retain documentation (contact details, EU declaration of conformity, technical documentation, certificates) for 10 years, provide information to competent authorities upon reasoned request including log access, cooperate in risk mitigation, and comply with registration obligations. They must terminate their mandate if the provider acts contrary to the Regulation and inform market surveillance authorities. Importers (Article 23) must verify conformity assessment, technical documentation, CE marking, EU declaration, instructions, and appointment of an authorised representative before placing systems on the market; refuse non-conforming or falsified systems; display their contact details; ensure safe storage/transport; retain documentation for 10 years; and cooperate with authorities. Distributors (Article 24) must verify CE marking, EU declaration, instructions, and provider/importer compliance before making systems available, and withhold non-conforming systems while notifying relevant parties.

nodes.title: Article 24 Obligations of distributors
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) details obligations for importers, distributors, and other actors in the AI value chain regarding high-risk AI systems. Importers must not place non-conforming or falsified systems on the market, inform relevant parties of risks, display their contact details, ensure storage/transport conditions preserve compliance, keep conformity documentation for 10 years, provide information to competent authorities upon request, and cooperate with authorities (Article 23). Distributors must verify CE marking, EU declaration of conformity, instructions, and provider/importer compliance before making systems available; refrain from distributing non-conforming systems; ensure safe storage/transport; take corrective actions including withdrawal or recall; inform authorities of risks; provide requested documentation; and cooperate with authorities (Article 24). Article 25 establishes that distributors, importers, deployers, or third parties become providers subject to Article 16 obligations if they rebrand a system, substantially modify it, or change its intended purpose making it high-risk.

nodes.title: Article 25 Responsibilities along the AI value chain
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers obligations across the AI value chain for high-risk AI systems. Distributors must ensure storage/transport conditions preserve compliance, take corrective actions for non-conforming systems, inform authorities of risks, provide documentation upon request, and cooperate with authorities (Article 24, paras 3-6). Article 25 defines when distributors, importers, deployers, or third parties become providers (rebranding, substantial modification, or changing intended purpose to high-risk), requires initial providers to cooperate with new providers by sharing documentation and technical access, designates product manufacturers as providers in certain cases, and mandates written agreements between providers and third-party suppliers (excluding free/open-source tools). The AI Office may develop voluntary model contract terms. IP rights are protected. Article 26 outlines deployer obligations: following instructions, assigning competent human oversight, ensuring relevant input data, monitoring operations, reporting risks/serious incidents, suspending use when needed, with specific provisions for law enforcement and financial institutions.

nodes.title: Article 26 Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers: the AI Office's role in developing voluntary model contract terms between high-risk AI providers and third-party suppliers, respecting IP rights and trade secrets. Article 26 details obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems: implementing technical/organizational measures, assigning competent human oversight, ensuring relevant input data, monitoring operations and reporting risks/serious incidents to providers and market surveillance authorities, retaining auto-generated logs for at least six months, informing workers and their representatives before workplace deployment, registration obligations for public authorities, using provider information for data protection impact assessments, and specific rules for post-remote biometric identification systems requiring judicial authorization, use limitations, documentation, annual reporting, and prohibitions on untargeted law enforcement use. Deployers must inform affected natural persons and cooperate with authorities. Article 27 introduces fundamental rights impact assessments required before deploying certain high-risk AI systems by public bodies or private entities providing public services, specifying required assessment components.

nodes.title: Article 27 Fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers obligations for deployers of high-risk AI systems. It requires documentation of each use in police files, availability to market surveillance and data protection authorities, and annual reports on post-remote biometric identification systems (excluding sensitive law enforcement data). Member States may impose stricter laws. Deployers must inform affected natural persons when AI is used in decisions about them and cooperate with competent authorities. Article 27 mandates a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) before deployment by public bodies, private entities providing public services, and certain Annex III deployers, detailing processes, usage duration, affected groups, risks, human oversight, and mitigation measures. The assessment applies to first use, can be updated or reused, must be notified to the market surveillance authority, and can cross-reference existing data protection impact assessments. The AI Office will provide a template. Section 4 (Article 28) requires Member States to designate notifying authorities for conformity assessment bodies.

This section of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) establishes obligations for all actors in the high-risk AI value chain. Article 16 lists providers' core duties (compliance, labeling, documentation, conformity assessment, CE marking, registration, corrective actions, accessibility). Article 17 mandates a documented quality management system covering compliance strategy, design, testing, data and risk management, post-market monitoring, incident reporting, and accountability, with proportionality for SMEs and integration options for financial institutions. Articles 18–19 require 10-year documentation retention and six-month log retention. Article 20 requires corrective actions and notifications for non-conformity; Article 21 mandates cooperation with authorities; Article 22 requires third-country providers to appoint an EU authorised representative. Articles 23–24 set importer and distributor verification and cooperation duties. Article 25 defines when actors become providers (rebranding, substantial modification), value-chain cooperation, and voluntary model contract terms. Article 26 details deployer obligations including human oversight, monitoring, worker information, and biometric identification rules. Article 27 requires Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments before certain deployments.

nodes.title: SECTION 4 Notifying authorities and notified bodies
Article 28 Notifying authorities
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers fundamental rights impact assessment obligations and notification procedures for AI conformity assessment bodies. It details requirements for deployers conducting fundamental rights impact assessments, including human oversight measures, risk mitigation arrangements, applicability to first use, notification duties to market surveillance authorities, and the ability to leverage existing data protection impact assessments. The AI Office is tasked with developing a template questionnaire. Section 4 addresses notifying authorities and notified bodies: Member States must designate notifying authorities responsible for assessing conformity assessment bodies, ensuring impartiality, confidentiality, adequate competent personnel, and no conflicts of interest. It establishes a single application and unified assessment procedure for bodies covered by multiple Union harmonisation legislations (Annex I Section A). Article 29 outlines application requirements for conformity assessment bodies, including accreditation certificates and documentation. Article 30 begins the notification procedure, allowing notification only of bodies meeting Article 31 requirements.

nodes.title: Article 29 Application of a conformity assessment body for notification
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), dated 27.07.2026, addresses notification procedures for conformity assessment bodies. It states that a notifying authority designated under Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I Section A also serves as the notifying authority for the unified assessment procedure, unless a Member State designates otherwise. Article 29 outlines the application process: conformity assessment bodies must apply to their Member State's notifying authority, including a description of activities, assessment modules, AI system types, and an accreditation certificate (or alternative documentary evidence if unavailable). Documents from existing designations under other Union legislation can support and expedite the procedure, and bodies undergoing unified assessment submit a single application. Documentation must be updated upon relevant changes to allow continuous compliance monitoring. Article 30 begins by stating notifying authorities may only notify bodies meeting Article 31 requirements.

nodes.title: Article 30 Notification procedure
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 28(9) through 31 regarding notification procedures for conformity assessment bodies. Article 28(9) specifies that notifying authorities designated under existing Union harmonisation legislation also serve for the unified assessment procedure unless otherwise designated. Article 29 outlines the application process for conformity assessment bodies seeking notification, requiring submission to their Member State's notifying authority with descriptions of activities, modules, AI system types, and accreditation certificates or alternative documentary evidence. It allows leveraging existing designations under other Union legislation. Article 30 details the notification procedure, including Commission notification via electronic tools based on Annex XIV codes, empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts amending Annex XIV, sets objection periods (two weeks with accreditation, two months without), and consultation processes for objections. Article 31 establishes requirements for notified bodies: national legal personality, organisational/quality/resource/process/cybersecurity requirements, and structural arrangements ensuring confidence in their performance.

nodes.title: Article 31 Requirements relating to notified bodies
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), Articles 30-34, covers the notification and operation of conformity assessment bodies for AI systems. Article 30 details notification procedures: notifying authorities must inform the Commission and Member States using an electronic tool based on Annex XIV codes, with provisions for delegated acts to amend the Annex. Notifications must include conformity assessment details and competence evidence, with objection periods of two weeks or two months. Article 31 outlines requirements for notified bodies: legal personality, organizational/cybersecurity standards, independence from providers and competitors, impartiality, confidentiality, proportionate procedures, liability insurance, professional integrity, internal competences, and participation in coordination/standardization. Article 32 establishes presumption of conformity through harmonised standards. Article 33 addresses subcontracting and subsidiaries, requiring compliance with Article 31, provider agreement, public lists, and five-year document retention. Article 34 specifies operational obligations, including verifying high-risk AI systems and minimizing burdens on SMEs.

nodes.title: Notified Bodies: Conformity Presumption, Subsidiaries, Subcontracting, and Operations
key_items: Article 32 Presumption of conformity with requirements relating to notified bodies
Article 33 Subsidiaries of notified bodies and subcontracting
nodes.summary: This page from Regulation 2024/1689 covers requirements for notified bodies. It notes their participation in coordination activities and European standardisation organisations (Article 31(12)). Article 32 establishes that conformity assessment bodies meeting relevant harmonised standards published in the Official Journal are presumed to comply with Article 31 requirements. Article 33 addresses subsidiaries and subcontracting: notified bodies must ensure subcontractors/subsidiaries meet Article 31 requirements and inform the notifying authority; they retain full responsibility; subcontracting requires provider agreement; subsidiary lists must be public; and assessment documents must be kept available for five years post-termination. Article 34 begins outlining operational obligations: verifying high-risk AI system conformity per Article 43, and avoiding unnecessary burdens by considering provider size, sector, structure, and system complexity—especially minimising costs for micro and small enterprises per Recommendation 2003/361/EC—while maintaining required rigour and protection levels.

nodes.title: Article 34 Operational obligations of notified bodies
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), Articles 32-36, covers requirements for notified bodies. Article 32 establishes presumption of conformity when bodies meet harmonised standards. Article 33 addresses subcontracting and subsidiaries, requiring compliance with Article 31, provider agreement, full responsibility, public lists of subsidiaries, and five-year document retention. Article 34 outlines operational obligations: verifying high-risk AI systems' conformity, minimising burdens especially for SMEs while maintaining rigour, and providing documentation to notifying authorities. Article 35 requires the Commission to assign unique identification numbers and maintain a public, up-to-date list of notified bodies. Article 36 governs changes to notifications: notifying authorities must inform the Commission of changes; cessation requires one year's notice with certificates valid nine months if another body assumes responsibility; and authorities must investigate non-compliance, potentially restricting, suspending, or withdrawing designations. Article 31 also mandates participation in coordination activities and standardisation awareness.

nodes.title: Article 35 Identification numbers and lists of notified bodies
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers obligations and procedures for notified bodies. Article 34(3) requires notified bodies to submit relevant documentation to notifying authorities for assessment, designation, notification, and monitoring. Article 35 mandates the Commission to assign a single identification number to each notified body and maintain an updated public list of notified bodies with their identification numbers and notified activities. Article 36 addresses changes to notifications: notifying authorities must inform the Commission and Member States of relevant changes via electronic tool; scope extensions follow Articles 29-30 procedures. If a notified body ceases activities, it must notify the authority and providers at least one year in advance; certificates remain valid for nine months if another body assumes responsibility and completes full reassessment. If a notified body fails requirements under Article 31, the notifying authority must investigate, allow the body to respond, and restrict, suspend, or withdraw designation accordingly, informing the Commission and Member States.

nodes.title: Article 36 Changes to notifications
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), Articles 34-37, covers obligations and procedures regarding notified bodies. Article 34 requires notified bodies to submit documentation to notifying authorities. Article 35 mandates the Commission to assign unique identification numbers and maintain a public list of notified bodies. Article 36 governs changes to notifications: cessation requires one year's notice with certificates remaining valid for nine months if another body assumes responsibility; notifying authorities must investigate non-compliance and may restrict, suspend or withdraw designations; affected providers must be informed within 10 days; files must be preserved; impact on certificates must be assessed and reported; conditions are detailed under which certificates remain valid during suspension, restriction (with notifying authority confirmations), or withdrawal (nine months extendable to 12). Article 37 empowers the Commission to investigate doubts about notified bodies' competence, requiring confidentiality, and allows it to adopt implementing acts to suspend, restrict, or withdraw designations if Member States fail to act.

nodes.title: Article 37 Challenge to the competence of notified bodies
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers provisions on notified bodies and standards. It outlines that certificates remain valid for nine months after a withdrawn designation under specific conditions (national authority confirms no risk; another notified body assumes responsibility within 12 months), extendable up to 12 months total. Article 37 addresses challenges to notified bodies' competence, authorizing Commission investigations, confidentiality obligations, and corrective measures including suspension or withdrawal via implementing acts. Article 38 mandates coordination among notified bodies through a sectoral group and knowledge exchange between notifying authorities. Article 39 allows third-country conformity assessment bodies to operate under EU agreements if they meet equivalent requirements. Article 40 establishes that compliance with harmonised standards published in the Official Journal presumes conformity with the Regulation's requirements, and directs the Commission to issue standardisation requests covering requirements, obligations, reporting/documentation, energy efficiency, and resource performance, consulting the Board and stakeholders.

nodes.title: Notified Bodies Coordination and Third-Country Conformity Assessment
key_items: Article 39 Conformity assessment bodies of third countries
nodes.summary: Article 38 requires the Commission to ensure coordination and cooperation among notified bodies involved in conformity assessments of high-risk AI systems through a sectoral group. Notifying authorities must ensure their notified bodies participate directly or via representatives, and the Commission facilitates exchange of knowledge and best practices. Article 39 permits conformity assessment bodies established in third countries, with which the Union has agreements, to act as notified bodies if they meet Article 31 requirements or ensure equivalent compliance. The page also begins Section 5 on standards, conformity assessment, certificates, and registration. Article 40 states that high-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models complying with harmonised standards published in the Official Journal are presumed conformant. The Commission must promptly issue standardisation requests covering all relevant requirements, including deliverables on reporting, documentation, resource/energy efficiency, and energy-efficient development of general-purpose AI models, consulting the Board, advisory forum, and stakeholders.

Section 4 of Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) establishes the framework for notifying authorities and notified bodies for high-risk AI conformity assessment. Article 28 requires Member States to designate impartial, competent notifying authorities and allows a unified procedure for bodies covered by multiple Union harmonisation laws. Article 29 details application requirements, including accreditation certificates or alternative evidence. Article 30 sets the notification procedure via a Commission electronic tool using Annex XIV codes, with objection periods and delegated act powers. Article 31 lists requirements for notified bodies (legal personality, independence, impartiality, confidentiality, cybersecurity, liability insurance, competence, standardisation participation). Article 32 presumes conformity through harmonised standards. Article 33 governs subcontracting and subsidiaries. Article 34 covers operational obligations, minimising SME burdens. Article 35 mandates unique identification numbers and a public list. Article 36 regulates changes, cessation, suspension, or withdrawal of notifications. Article 37 enables Commission challenges to competence. Articles 38–39 address coordination among notified bodies and recognition of third-country bodies.

nodes.title: SECTION 5 Standards, conformity assessment, certificates, registration
Article 40 Harmonised standards and standardisation deliverables
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 38-41. Article 38 mandates the Commission to ensure coordination between notified bodies for high-risk AI systems via a sectoral group, with notifying authorities ensuring participation and knowledge exchange. Article 39 permits third-country conformity assessment bodies to operate as notified bodies under Union agreements if they meet equivalent requirements. Article 40 establishes that high-risk AI systems and general-purpose AI models complying with harmonised standards published in the Official Journal are presumed conformant; the Commission must issue standardisation requests covering requirements, including resource/energy efficiency, after consulting the Board and stakeholders, promoting investment, innovation, legal certainty, global cooperation, and multi-stakeholder governance aligned with Union values. Article 41 allows the Commission to adopt implementing acts establishing common specifications when standardisation requests are not accepted by European standardisation organisations. A footnote references Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 on European standardisation.

nodes.title: Article 41 Common specifications
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers standardisation and conformity provisions. It mandates the Commission to issue standardisation requests to European standardisation organisations for clear, consistent harmonised standards ensuring high-risk AI systems and general-purpose AI models meet regulatory requirements, promoting innovation, legal certainty, global cooperation, and multi-stakeholder governance. Article 41 permits the Commission to adopt implementing acts establishing common specifications when harmonised standards are unavailable, delayed, insufficient regarding fundamental rights, or non-compliant, with conformity presumption applying; providers deviating must justify equivalent technical solutions, and Member States may flag inadequacies. Article 42 grants presumption of conformity for high-risk AI systems trained on representative data (Article 10(4)) and those certified under cybersecurity schemes (Regulation 2019/881 or 2024/2847) for Article 15 requirements. Article 43 outlines conformity assessment procedures for Annex III point 1 systems, allowing choice between internal control (Annex VI) or notified body assessment (Annex VII), with Annex VII mandatory when harmonised standards/common specifications are absent, unapplied, or restricted.

nodes.title: Article 42 Presumption of conformity with certain requirements
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers Articles 42 and 43. Article 42 establishes presumptions of conformity: (1) high-risk AI systems trained/tested on data reflecting their intended geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting are presumed to comply with Article 10(4); (2) systems certified under cybersecurity schemes per Regulation (EU) 2019/881 are presumed compliant with Article 15 cybersecurity requirements; and (3) systems falling under Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 meeting its Article 12(1) conditions are deemed compliant with Article 15. Article 43 outlines conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III point 1: providers using harmonised standards or common specifications may choose between internal control (Annex VI) or quality management system and technical documentation assessment with notified body involvement (Annex VII). Annex VII is mandatory when harmonised standards/common specifications don't exist, aren't applied fully, or are published with restrictions.

nodes.title: Article 43 Conformity assessment
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 42-44. Article 42 establishes presumptions of conformity: high-risk AI systems trained on representative data presume compliance with Article 10(4); systems certified under cybersecurity schemes (Regulation 2019/881) or falling under Regulation 2024/2847 presume compliance with Article 15 cybersecurity requirements. Article 43 details conformity assessment procedures: providers of Annex III point 1 systems choose between internal control (Annex VI) or notified body assessment (Annex VII), with specified conditions requiring Annex VII; points 2-8 systems use internal control; systems under Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I Section A) follow those procedures incorporating Section 2 requirements. Notified bodies must apply for designation by 28 January 2028. Substantial modifications trigger new assessments, excluding pre-determined changes. The Commission may adopt delegated acts updating annexes. Article 44 addresses certificates: issued in understandable language, valid up to 5 years (Annex I) or 4 years (Annex III), renewable upon reassessment.

nodes.title: Article 44 Certificates
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems. It specifies that systems covered by both Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I Section A) and Annex III categories must follow the relevant harmonisation procedure. Substantial modifications trigger new conformity assessments, except for pre-determined changes documented at initial assessment for continuously learning systems. The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts amending Annexes VI and VII and paragraphs 1-2 based on technical progress and risk considerations. Article 44 addresses certificates: language requirements, validity periods (max 5 years for Annex I, 4 years for Annex III, renewable), and suspension/withdrawal procedures with appeal rights when systems no longer meet requirements. Article 45 outlines notified bodies' information obligations toward notifying authorities (certificates, refusals, scope changes, market surveillance requests) and other notified bodies (sharing approvals, refusals, negative/positive assessment results), while maintaining confidentiality per Article 78.

nodes.title: Article 45 Information obligations of notified bodies
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers provisions on notified bodies and conformity assessment for high-risk AI systems. It specifies that notified bodies may suspend, withdraw, or restrict certificates when AI systems no longer meet requirements, allowing corrective action, and mandates an appeal procedure. Article 45 outlines notified bodies' information obligations: informing notifying authorities about certificates, refusals, restrictions, scope changes, and market surveillance requests; sharing information with other notified bodies about refused/withdrawn approvals and negative assessment results; and maintaining confidentiality per Article 78. Article 46 establishes derogations from conformity assessment, allowing market surveillance authorities to authorize placing high-risk AI systems on the market for exceptional reasons (public security, health, environment, infrastructure). Law enforcement/civil protection may use systems urgently without prior authorization, requesting it after. Authorizations require compliance with Section 2, must be notified to Commission and Member States, are deemed justified after 15 days without objection, and can be withdrawn if the Commission deems them unjustified following consultations.

nodes.title: Article 46 Derogation from conformity assessment procedure
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers three articles on high-risk AI systems. Article 46 permits derogation from conformity assessment: market surveillance authorities may authorize placing specific high-risk AI systems on the market for exceptional reasons (public security, health, environment, infrastructure); law enforcement/civil protection may act without prior authorization in urgent cases; authorizations require notification to the Commission and Member States, with a 15-day objection window, Commission consultation procedures, and withdrawal if unjustified. Article 47 requires providers to draw up a written EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system, retained for 10 years, stating compliance with Section 2 requirements, translated appropriately, consolidated with other applicable Union legislation, with Commission empowered to amend Annex V via delegated acts. Article 48 governs CE marking under Regulation 765/2008, including digital CE marking for digitally-provided systems, requiring visible, legible, indelible affixation or placement on packaging/documentation.

nodes.title: Article 47 EU declaration of conformity
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers provisions on conformity for high-risk AI systems. Point 7 states that for high-risk AI systems linked to products under Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I, Section A), only the derogations in that legislation apply. Article 47 requires providers to draw up a written, machine-readable EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system, retain it for 10 years, submit it on request, include Annex V information, translate it appropriately, consolidate it when multiple Union laws apply, assume compliance responsibility, and keep it updated. It empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts amending Annex V. Article 48 governs CE marking, applying principles from Regulation (EC) No 765/2008, requiring digital CE marking for digitally provided systems via accessible means, and mandating visible, legible, indelible affixation on the system, packaging, or documentation.

nodes.title: Article 48 CE marking
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 47-49 regarding compliance of high-risk AI systems. Article 47 (EU Declaration of Conformity) requires providers to draw up a written, machine-readable declaration kept available for 10 years, containing Annex V information, translated appropriately, consolidated with other Union harmonisation legislation where applicable, and empowers the Commission to amend Annex V via delegated acts. Article 48 (CE Marking) mandates compliance with Regulation 765/2008, allows digital CE marking for digitally-provided systems, requires visible/legible/indelible affixing (or on packaging), inclusion of the notified body's identification number where applicable, and indicates compliance with other relevant Union law. Article 49 (Registration) requires providers, authorised representatives, and public-authority deployers to register themselves and high-risk AI systems (Annex III) in the EU database (Article 71), with special secure non-public sections for law enforcement, migration, asylum, and border control systems, and national-level registration for point 2 Annex III systems. Also notes derogations for products under Section A of Annex I.

nodes.title: Article 49 Registration
key_items: 5. High-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III shall be registered at national level.
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers CE marking and transparency obligations. Article 48(4-5) requires the CE marking to be followed by the notified body's identification number where applicable, and to indicate compliance with other relevant Union laws. Article 49 mandates registration in the EU database (Article 71) by providers, authorised representatives, and public-authority deployers before placing high-risk AI systems (Annex III) on the market, with exceptions for point 2 of Annex III (national registration). Law enforcement, migration, asylum, and border control AI systems register in a secure non-public section with limited information, accessible only to the Commission and designated national authorities. Article 50 establishes transparency obligations: informing persons when interacting with AI, marking synthetic audio/image/video/text as artificially generated in machine-readable format, informing people subject to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems, and disclosing deep fakes, with exceptions for law enforcement and artistic works.

This section (Articles 38-49 of EU Regulation 2024/1689, the AI Act) establishes standards, conformity assessment, certification, and registration rules for high-risk AI systems. It covers coordination among notified bodies (Art. 38) and recognition of third-country bodies (Art. 39). Articles 40-41 address harmonised standards granting presumption of conformity and allow the Commission to adopt common specifications when standards are lacking. Article 42 presumes conformity for systems trained on representative data or certified under cybersecurity schemes. Article 43 details conformity assessment procedures (internal control via Annex VI or notified body assessment via Annex VII), rules on substantial modifications, and delegated acts. Article 44 governs certificate language, validity, suspension, and appeals. Article 45 sets notified bodies' information-sharing duties. Article 46 permits exceptional derogations from conformity assessment. Articles 47-48 require an EU declaration of conformity and CE marking (including digital). Article 49 mandates registration of providers, deployers, and systems in the EU database, with secure sections for sensitive uses.

Chapter III of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) governs high-risk AI systems across five sections. Section 1 (Arts. 6-8) classifies high-risk systems based on Annex I harmonisation legislation and Annex III use cases, with exceptions for minimal-risk tasks, and empowers the Commission to amend Annex III. Section 2 (Arts. 8-15) sets requirements: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity. Section 3 (Arts. 16-27) assigns obligations to providers (compliance, quality management, documentation retention, corrective actions, EU representatives), importers, distributors, and deployers (monitoring, worker information, Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments), defining when actors become providers. Section 4 (Arts. 28-39) establishes notifying authorities and notified bodies, covering designation, application, notification procedures, requirements, subcontracting, identification, and third-country recognition. Section 5 (Arts. 38-49) addresses harmonised standards, common specifications, conformity assessment procedures, certificates, derogations, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, and registration in the EU database. It also includes reporting obligations on biometric identification use.

nodes.title: CHAPTER IV TRANSPARENCY OBLIGATIONS FOR PROVIDERS AND DEPLOYERS OF CERTAIN AI SYSTEMS
key_items: Article 50 Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems
nodes.summary: This excerpt from Regulation 2024/1689 covers Chapter IV on transparency obligations and begins Chapter V on general-purpose AI models. Article 50 requires: (1) providers to inform users when interacting with AI systems unless obvious; (2) providers of generative AI to mark synthetic audio, image, video, or text outputs as machine-readable and detectable; (3) deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems to inform exposed persons and comply with data protection laws; (4) deployers to disclose deep fakes and AI-generated text on public interest matters, with exceptions for artistic works and human-reviewed content. Information must be clear, timely, and accessible. Law enforcement exceptions apply throughout. The Commission will facilitate codes of practice and may adopt implementing acts if inadequate. Chapter V, Article 51 classifies general-purpose AI models as having systemic risk based on high-impact capabilities measured via benchmarks or a Commission decision referencing Annex XIII criteria.

nodes.title: CHAPTER V GENERAL-PURPOSE AI MODELS
SECTION 1 Classification rules
key_items: Article 51 Classification of general-purpose AI models as general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers transparency and general-purpose AI model rules. It requires deployers of AI generating public-interest text to disclose artificial generation, with exceptions for law enforcement or human-reviewed content. Information must be clear, accessible, and provided at first interaction. The Commission will facilitate codes of practice for implementation. Chapter V classifies general-purpose AI models as having systemic risk based on high-impact capabilities, with a presumption threshold of 10^25 FLOPs for training computation. Providers must notify the Commission within two weeks when thresholds are met, and may contest classification. The Commission can designate models ex officio, maintain a public list, and reassess upon provider request (minimum six months after designation). Provider obligations include maintaining technical documentation (Annex XI), providing information to downstream AI system integrators (Annex XII), implementing copyright compliance policies aligned with Directive 2019/790, and publishing a summary of training content per an AI Office template.

nodes.title: SECTION 2 Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
key_items: Article 53 Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
1. Providers of general-purpose AI models shall:
Article 54 Authorised representatives of providers of general-purpose AI models
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers rules for general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. Article 52(5-6) allows providers to request reassessment of systemic risk designation six months after designation, and requires the Commission to publish a list of GPAI models with systemic risk. Article 53 sets obligations for GPAI providers: maintaining technical documentation (Annex XI), providing information to downstream AI system integrators (Annex XII), implementing a copyright compliance policy including honoring Article 4(3) of Directive 2019/790 opt-outs, and publishing a training content summary per an AI Office template. Open-source models are exempt from documentation duties unless they pose systemic risks. Codes of practice and harmonised standards provide presumption of conformity. Article 54 requires non-EU providers to appoint EU-based authorised representatives with specified tasks (verification, documentation retention for 10 years, cooperation), with open-source exemptions. Article 55 begins listing additional obligations for systemic-risk GPAI providers, including state-of-the-art model evaluation and adversarial testing.

nodes.title: SECTION 3 Obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
key_items: Article 55 Obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) outlines obligations for authorised representatives of general-purpose AI model providers, including verifying technical documentation (Annex XI), retaining it for 10 years, providing information to the AI Office upon request, and cooperating with authorities. The mandate empowers representatives to be addressed on compliance issues and must be terminated if the provider acts contrary to obligations. These obligations exempt providers of free and open-source models unless they pose systemic risks. Article 55 details additional obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk: performing standardised model evaluations with adversarial testing, assessing/mitigating Union-level systemic risks, reporting serious incidents to the AI Office, and ensuring cybersecurity. Providers may rely on codes of practice or harmonised standards for presumption of conformity, or demonstrate alternative compliance. Confidentiality applies per Article 78. Article 56 tasks the AI Office with facilitating Union-level codes of practice covering Articles 53 and 55 obligations.

nodes.title: SECTION 4 Codes of practice
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, including risk assessment and mitigation at Union level, tracking and reporting serious incidents to the AI Office, and ensuring cybersecurity. Providers may use codes of practice or harmonised standards to demonstrate compliance, with confidentiality protections applying. Article 56 details codes of practice: the AI Office facilitates their creation, covering obligations under Articles 53 and 55, including information updates, training content summaries, systemic risk identification, and risk management measures. Stakeholders including providers, authorities, civil society, and experts may participate. Codes must set objectives, KPIs, and reporting requirements. The Commission monitors and assesses adequacy, and may adopt implementing acts if codes are not finalised by 2 August 2025. Article 57 requires Member States to establish AI regulatory sandboxes by 2 August 2027, with provisions for regional, EU-level, and EDPS sandboxes, prioritizing SMEs.

Chapter V of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) governs general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. Section 1 establishes classification rules, designating GPAI models with systemic risk based on high-impact capabilities, with a presumption threshold of 10^25 FLOPs. Providers must notify the Commission within two weeks of meeting thresholds, may contest classification, and request reassessment six months after designation; the Commission maintains a public list. Section 2 sets provider obligations: maintaining technical documentation (Annex XI), informing downstream integrators (Annex XII), implementing copyright compliance aligned with Directive 2019/790, and publishing training content summaries. Open-source models are exempt unless posing systemic risk. Non-EU providers must appoint EU-based authorised representatives with defined duties. Section 3 adds obligations for systemic-risk GPAI providers: standardised evaluations with adversarial testing, Union-level risk mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity. Section 4 details codes of practice facilitated by the AI Office, with Commission oversight, implementing acts if unfinalised by August 2025, and establishes AI regulatory sandboxes by August 2027.

nodes.title: CHAPTER VI MEASURES IN SUPPORT OF INNOVATION
Article 57 AI regulatory sandboxes
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers two main areas. First, it states that if a code of practice for AI obligations under Articles 53 and 55 is not finalized by August 2025 or deemed inadequate, the Commission may adopt implementing acts with common rules. Second, Chapter VI (Article 57) establishes AI regulatory sandboxes: Member States must set up at least one national sandbox by August 2027, with options for regional, joint, or Union-level sandboxes (by the European Data Protection Supervisor or AI Office). It details sandbox objectives (legal certainty, innovation, SME market access, regulatory learning), operation (controlled environments, real-world testing, guidance, exit reports usable for conformity assessments), liability rules (providers remain liable for damages but exempt from administrative fines if compliant with sandbox terms), cooperation requirements, annual reporting obligations, and a Commission-developed single interface. Article 58 mandates Commission implementing acts specifying detailed arrangements, eligibility, procedures, and participant terms.

nodes.title: Article 58 Detailed arrangements for, and functioning of, AI regulatory sandboxes
key_items: 2. The implementing acts referred to in paragraph 1 shall ensure:
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers provisions on AI regulatory sandboxes. It outlines coordination among national competent authorities, the European Data Protection Supervisor, and the AI Office, including sharing best practices and maintaining a public list of sandboxes. It mandates annual and final reporting on sandbox progress, results, and lessons learned. The Commission must create a single interface for stakeholder interaction. Article 58 requires implementing acts to specify detailed arrangements—eligibility, procedures, participant terms, and governance—ensuring transparency, free SME access, broad participation, flexibility, uniform EU-wide recognition, limited participation periods, and tools for testing AI dimensions like accuracy and cybersecurity. Providers should be directed to pre-deployment services, Digital Innovation Hubs, and testing facilities. Real-world testing requires agreed safeguards. Article 59 permits further processing of lawfully collected personal data within sandboxes for developing AI systems serving substantial public interest in areas like public health, environment, energy, transport, and public administration.

nodes.title: Article 59 Further processing of personal data for developing certain AI systems in the public interest in the AI regulatory sandbox
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers AI regulatory sandboxes and real-world testing provisions. It outlines conditions for sandbox participation, including time limits, facilitation of testing tools/infrastructure, and directing SMEs/startups to pre-deployment and value-adding services like European Digital Innovation Hubs. It addresses safeguards for real-world testing within sandboxes to protect fundamental rights, health, and safety. Article 59 permits further processing of personal data in sandboxes for developing AI systems serving substantial public interest (public safety/health, environment, energy, transport, public administration), subject to conditions: necessity, risk monitoring, isolated data environments, restricted sharing, data protection measures, logging, documentation, and public summaries. Special provisions apply for law enforcement purposes. Article 60 governs testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions outside sandboxes, requiring a real-world testing plan (detailed via Commission implementing acts), market surveillance authority approval (with 30-day tacit approval where permitted), compliance with ethical reviews, and allowing partnerships with deployers before market placement.

nodes.title: Article 60 Testing of high-risk AI systems in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) addresses personal data processing provisions and governs testing of high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes.
