Article 60 establishes that providers may conduct such testing before market placement, subject to conditions including: a Commission-specified real-world testing plan approved by market surveillance authorities (with 30-day tacit approval); registration in EU databases with unique identifiers; EU establishment or legal representation; data transfer safeguards; maximum six-month duration (extendable once); protection of vulnerable subjects; cooperation agreements with deployers; informed consent (with law enforcement exceptions); qualified oversight; and reversibility of AI outputs. Subjects may withdraw consent without detriment and request data deletion. Market surveillance authorities have inspection powers. Serious incidents must be reported with mitigation or suspension, and providers remain liable for damages. Article 60a (M1 amendment) allows Member States to permit real-world testing of high-risk AI systems covered by Section B of Annex I harmonisation legislation to verify conformity with Articles 8–15.

nodes.title: Article 60a Testing of high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section B of Annex I in real-world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes
nodes.summary: This text from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers provisions on testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions. It outlines requirements including: oversight by qualified persons, reversibility of AI decisions, subjects' right to withdraw consent without detriment and request data deletion, market surveillance authorities' powers (inspections, information requests), mandatory reporting of serious incidents with immediate mitigation or suspension, notification duties regarding suspension/termination, and provider liability under Union/national law. Article 60a (M1 amendment) permits real-world testing of high-risk AI systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I Section B) outside regulatory sandboxes, requiring Member States to adopt frameworks notified to the Commission, ensure cooperation among national authorities, include mandatory testing plans agreed with competent authorities, comply with Article 60(2)-(9) provisions, provide governance/accountability arrangements, and protect health, safety and fundamental rights. Article 61 begins addressing informed consent requirements for testing subjects, requiring clear prior information.

nodes.title: Article 61 Informed consent to participate in testing in real world conditions outside AI regulatory sandboxes
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers provisions on real-world AI testing and support for SMEs. It outlines Member States' options to allow real-world testing frameworks, requiring Commission notification, inter-authority cooperation, mandatory testing plans, governance arrangements, and protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights, while complying with Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I, Section B). Article 61 details informed consent requirements for testing subjects outside AI regulatory sandboxes, including information on testing nature, conditions, rights to withdraw, reversal arrangements, and identification numbers; consent must be documented and copied to subjects. Article 62 sets measures supporting providers and deployers, especially SMEs and start-ups: priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes, tailored awareness and training, communication channels for guidance, facilitation of standardisation participation, and proportionate reduction of conformity assessment fees based on size and market considerations.

nodes.title: Article 62 Measures for providers and deployers, in particular SMEs, including start-ups
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers several provisions. It details informed consent requirements for subjects in real-world AI testing, including information on testing nature, conditions, participant rights (refusal/withdrawal), reversal of AI decisions, and identification numbers, requiring dated documentation. Article 62 outlines measures supporting SMEs and start-ups, including priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes, awareness/training activities, communication channels, standardization participation, and proportionate conformity assessment fees. It assigns the AI Office tasks like providing templates, maintaining an information platform, awareness campaigns, and promoting public procurement best practices. Article 63 permits SMEs without partner/linked enterprises to comply with quality management requirements in a simplified manner per Commission guidelines, without exempting them from other obligations. Chapter VII begins governance provisions, establishing the AI Office under Article 64 to develop Union AI expertise, with Member State cooperation and adequate resource allocation for enforcement.

nodes.title: Article 63 Derogations for specific operators
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 outlines AI Office actions and governance provisions. The AI Office must: provide standardised templates for areas covered by the Regulation as requested by the Board; develop and maintain a single information platform for operators across the Union; organise communication campaigns to raise awareness of obligations; and evaluate and promote best practices in public procurement for AI systems. Article 63 provides derogations allowing SMEs and start-ups (without partner or linked enterprises per Recommendation 2003/361/EC) to comply with certain quality management system elements under Article 17 in a simplified manner, with Commission-developed guidelines, without reducing protection levels. This does not exempt them from other obligations (Articles 9-15, 72, 73). Chapter VII, Section 1 establishes Union-level governance: the Commission develops AI expertise through the AI Office; Member States must facilitate its tasks; and the AI Office must receive adequate resources for enforcement duties.

Chapter VI of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) establishes measures supporting AI innovation. Article 57 requires Member States to create AI regulatory sandboxes by August 2027, defining their objectives, operation, liability rules, cooperation, and reporting. Article 58 mandates Commission implementing acts detailing sandbox arrangements, eligibility, SME access, and testing tools. Article 59 permits further processing of lawfully collected personal data within sandboxes for public-interest AI development (health, environment, energy, transport, administration), with strict safeguards and special law enforcement provisions. Article 60 governs real-world testing of high-risk AI outside sandboxes, requiring approved testing plans, EU registration, time limits, informed consent, oversight, incident reporting, and provider liability. Article 60a (M1 amendment) extends real-world testing to high-risk AI under Annex I Section B harmonisation legislation. Article 61 sets informed consent requirements. Article 62 provides SME/start-up support (priority sandbox access, training, reduced fees). Article 63 allows simplified compliance derogations for SMEs.

nodes.title: CHAPTER VII GOVERNANCE
SECTION 1 Governance at Union level
Article 64 AI Office
key_items: 3. The AI Office shall undertake the following actions:
nodes.summary: This excerpt from Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) outlines: AI Office duties (standardised templates, single information platform, awareness campaigns, promoting best practices in AI public procurement); Article 63 derogations allowing SMEs and start-ups without partner/linked enterprises to comply with quality management system elements in a simplified manner per Commission guidelines, without exemption from other obligations. Chapter VII on Governance establishes the AI Office (Article 64), with the Commission developing Union AI expertise, Member States facilitating its tasks, and adequate resources allocated. Article 65 establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Board, composed of one representative per Member State with EDPS as observer and AI Office attending non-voting; representatives serve three-year renewable terms, must have competences, act as single contact points, and ensure coordination. Rules of procedure are adopted by two-thirds majority. The Board establishes two standing sub-groups for market surveillance (acting as ADCO) and notified bodies, plus optional additional sub-groups.

nodes.title: Article 65 Establishment and structure of the European Artificial Intelligence Board
nodes.summary: This text contains Articles 65 and 66 of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act). Article 65 establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Board, composed of one representative per Member State, with the European Data Protection Supervisor as observer and the AI Office attending without voting. It details representative designation (three-year renewable terms), required competences, single contact point roles, and adoption of rules of procedure by two-thirds majority. The Board must establish two standing sub-groups for market surveillance (acting as ADCO under Regulation 2019/1020) and notifying authorities, with option for additional sub-groups. It mandates objectivity, chairmanship by a Member State representative, and AI Office secretariat support. Article 66 outlines the Board's tasks to advise the Commission and Member States for consistent application: coordinating national authorities, sharing expertise, advising on general-purpose AI model enforcement, harmonising administrative practices (conformity derogations, sandboxes, real-world testing), and issuing recommendations on codes of conduct, regulation evaluation, serious incidents, EU database, delegated acts, and technical standards.

nodes.title: Article 66 Tasks of the Board
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers governance structures. Article 65 (partial) specifies the Board's organization, ensuring objectivity, with Member State chairmanship and AI Office secretariat support. Article 66 outlines the Board's tasks: advising the Commission and Member States, coordinating national authorities, sharing expertise, advising on general-purpose AI enforcement, harmonizing administrative practices, issuing recommendations on codes of conduct, evaluation, technical standards, AI literacy, value chain accountability, Annex III amendments, cooperation with Union bodies and third countries, developing expertise, supporting regulatory sandboxes, international matters, and opinions on qualified alerts. Article 67 establishes an advisory forum providing technical expertise with balanced stakeholder representation (industry, SMEs, civil society, academia), Commission-appointed members with two-year terms, permanent members (FRA, ENISA, CEN, CENELEC, ETSI), biannual meetings, co-chairs, subgroups, and annual public reports. Article 68 (partial) mandates the Commission to establish a scientific panel of independent experts via implementing act to support enforcement.

nodes.title: Article 67 Advisory forum
nodes.summary: This excerpt from Regulation 2024/1689 covers Articles 67 and 68. Article 67 establishes an Advisory Forum to provide technical expertise to the Board and Commission. It specifies: balanced stakeholder membership (industry, startups, SMEs, civil society, academia, balancing commercial/non-commercial interests); Commission appointment based on AI expertise; two-year renewable terms (max four years); permanent members including the Fundamental Rights Agency, ENISA, CEN, CENELEC, and ETSI; adoption of rules of procedure; election of two co-chairs with two-year renewable terms; biannual meetings with the option to invite external experts; preparation of opinions, recommendations, and contributions upon request; ability to form standing or temporary sub-groups; and publication of an annual activity report. Article 68 mandates that the Commission establish, via implementing act under the examination procedure of Article 98(2), a Scientific Panel of independent experts to support enforcement activities under the Regulation.

nodes.title: Article 68 Scientific panel of independent experts
nodes.summary: This text from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers Articles 67-70. Article 67 establishes an Advisory Forum providing technical expertise to the Board and Commission, detailing its balanced stakeholder membership (industry, SMEs, civil society, academia), two-year renewable terms, permanent members (Fundamental Rights Agency, ENISA, CEN, CENELEC, ETSI), co-chair election, biannual meetings, ability to issue opinions and form sub-groups, and annual public reporting. Article 68 establishes a Scientific Panel of Independent Experts via implementing act to support enforcement, specifying selection criteria (AI expertise, independence, objectivity), tasks (alerting systemic risks, developing evaluation tools, classifying general-purpose AI models, supporting market surveillance and Union safeguard procedures), and conflict-of-interest management. Article 69 allows Member States to access the expert pool for enforcement, potentially paying fees, with Commission facilitation. Article 70 requires Member States to designate independent national competent authorities (notifying and market surveillance), communicate their details to the Commission, and establish a single point of contact by 2 August 2025.

nodes.title: Article 69 Access to the pool of experts by the Member States
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers provisions on the scientific panel and national competent authorities. Article 68(5) requires the implementing act to detail conditions and procedures for the scientific panel to issue alerts and seek AI Office assistance. Article 69 allows Member States to call upon scientific panel experts to support enforcement, potentially subject to fees equivalent to Commission remuneration rates, with the Commission facilitating timely access and coordinating with Union AI testing support under Article 84. Article 70 (Section 2) requires each Member State to establish or designate at least one notifying authority and one market surveillance authority as national competent authorities, operating independently and impartially. Member States must notify the Commission of these authorities and their tasks, publicly share contact information electronically by 2 August 2025, and designate a market surveillance authority as the single point of contact. The Commission will publish a list of these single points of contact.

This section of the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) establishes governance structures at Union level. Article 64 creates the AI Office within the Commission to develop Union AI expertise, with Member State support and adequate resourcing. Article 65 establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Board, composed of one representative per Member State (with EDPS as observer and AI Office non-voting), detailing three-year renewable terms, required competences, two-thirds majority rules of procedure, mandatory sub-groups for market surveillance (ADCO) and notifying authorities, Member State chairmanship, and AI Office secretariat. Article 66 lists the Board's advisory and coordination tasks, including harmonising practices, issuing recommendations on codes of conduct, standards, Annex III amendments, and international cooperation. Article 67 establishes an Advisory Forum with balanced stakeholder representation and permanent members (FRA, ENISA, CEN, CENELEC, ETSI). Article 68 creates a Scientific Panel of Independent Experts via implementing act. Article 69 grants Member States access to this expert pool, potentially for a fee.

nodes.title: SECTION 2 National competent authorities
key_items: Article 70 Designation of national competent authorities and single points of contact
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 69-71. Article 69 governs Member States' access to the scientific panel of experts for enforcement, with possible fees payable at Commission-equivalent rates, and tasks the Commission with facilitating timely access and coordination with Union AI testing support. Section 2, Article 70 requires Member States to designate at least one notifying and one market surveillance authority as national competent authorities, operating independently and impartially, with a designated single point of contact communicated to the Commission by 2 August 2025. It mandates adequate technical, financial, and human resources with expertise in AI, data protection, cybersecurity, and fundamental rights, biennial reporting to the Commission, cybersecurity measures, confidentiality compliance, and guidance to SMEs/startups. The European Data Protection Supervisor supervises Union institutions. Chapter VIII, Article 71 establishes an EU database for high-risk AI systems maintained by the Commission in collaboration with Member States, consulting experts and the Board on specifications.

Chapter VII of the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) establishes AI governance structures. Section 1 covers Union-level governance: Article 64 creates the AI Office within the Commission; Article 65 establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Board with Member State representatives, outlining composition, terms, voting rules, and mandatory sub-groups for market surveillance and notifying authorities; Article 66 defines the Board's advisory and coordination tasks, including harmonising practices and issuing recommendations; Article 67 sets up a multi-stakeholder Advisory Forum with permanent members (FRA, ENISA, CEN, CENELEC, ETSI); Article 68 creates a Scientific Panel of Independent Experts; Article 69 grants Member States access to this panel, possibly for a fee, with Commission coordination. Section 2 addresses national competent authorities: Article 70 requires Member States to designate notifying and market surveillance authorities by 2 August 2025, ensuring independence, adequate resources, expertise, biennial reporting, cybersecurity, confidentiality, and SME guidance, with EDPS supervising Union institutions.

nodes.title: CHAPTER VIII EU DATABASE FOR HIGH-RISK AI SYSTEMS
key_items: Article 71 EU database for high-risk AI systems listed in AnnexIII
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers three main areas. Article 70 continuation outlines requirements for national competent authorities: Member States must provide adequate technical, financial, human resources, and personnel with expertise in AI, data protection, cybersecurity, fundamental rights, and safety. Authorities must ensure cybersecurity, respect confidentiality (Article 78), report biennially to the Commission on resources starting August 2025, exchange experiences, and may offer guidance to SMEs and startups. The European Data Protection Supervisor supervises EU institutions. Chapter VIII, Article 71 establishes an EU database for high-risk AI systems, maintained by the Commission, with data entered by providers, authorised representatives, or public-authority deployers. Information is publicly accessible except for law enforcement/migration cases, with personal data limited to responsible contacts; the Commission acts as controller. Chapter IX, Article 72 requires providers to establish proportionate post-market monitoring systems to collect and analyse performance data ensuring continuous compliance, excluding sensitive law-enforcement operational data.

nodes.title: CHAPTER IX POST-MARKET MONITORING, INFORMATION SHARING AND MARKET SURVEILLANCE
SECTION 1 Post-market monitoring
key_items: Article 72 Post-market monitoring by providers and post-market monitoring plan for high-risk AI systems
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers provisions on the EU database for high-risk AI systems and post-market monitoring. It specifies that providers, authorised representatives, and public-authority deployers enter data per Annex VIII sections into the EU database, with most information being publicly accessible, user-friendly, and machine-readable, while Article 60 data is restricted to market surveillance authorities and the Commission. Personal data is limited to responsible registrants, with the Commission as controller providing technical support and ensuring accessibility compliance. Chapter IX requires providers to establish proportionate post-market monitoring systems and plans (part of Annex IV documentation), with Commission guidance due by 2 September 2027; integration with existing Union harmonisation legislation systems is permitted. Article 73 mandates reporting of serious incidents to market surveillance authorities: within 15 days generally, within 2 days for widespread infringements, and within 10 days in case of death, timed from establishing a causal link.

nodes.title: SECTION 2 Sharing of information on serious incidents
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers post-market monitoring, incident reporting, and enforcement. Article 72(3-4) requires providers to maintain a post-market monitoring plan based on a Commission template (due by September 2027), allowing integration with existing monitoring systems under Union harmonisation legislation for consistency. Article 73 mandates providers to report serious incidents to market surveillance authorities: generally within 15 days, within 2 days for widespread infringements, and within 10 days for deaths. Providers may submit initial incomplete reports, must investigate and cooperate with authorities without altering the AI system, and the Commission will issue guidance by August 2025. Specific rules apply to systems under other EU laws (e.g., medical device regulations). Article 74 extends Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 to AI systems, requires annual reporting on competition-relevant findings and prohibited practices, designates sectoral market surveillance authorities, and allows remote exercise of certain enforcement powers.

nodes.title: SECTION 3 Enforcement
Article 74 Market surveillance and control of AI systems in the Union market
nodes.summary: This text covers Articles 74 and 75 of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), addressing enforcement and market surveillance of AI systems. Article 74 establishes that Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applies to AI systems, requires market surveillance authorities to report annually to the Commission on competition issues and prohibited practices, and designates appropriate market surveillance authorities for various categories: high-risk AI tied to Union harmonisation legislation, financial institutions, law enforcement/border/justice uses, and EU institutions (overseen by the EDPS). It permits remote exercise of powers, joint investigations coordinated by the AI Office, and grants authorities access to documentation, datasets, and—under conditions—source code, with confidentiality safeguards. Article 75 (as amended) grants the AI Office exclusive competence over supervision and enforcement for AI systems built on general-purpose AI models by the same provider (with specified exceptions regarding Annex I/III systems, law enforcement, financial, and justice administration), and for AI systems integrated into very large online platforms or search engines under Regulation 2022/2065.

nodes.title: Article 75 Market surveillance and control of AI systems and mutual assistance
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers market surveillance provisions for AI systems. Article 74 (paragraphs 12-14) grants market surveillance authorities access to providers' documentation, training/testing datasets (including via APIs), and source code under reasoned requests when necessary for conformity assessment and other methods are exhausted, subject to confidentiality obligations. Article 75 establishes the AI Office's exclusive competence over AI systems based on general-purpose AI models from the same provider (with exceptions) and systems integrated into very large online platforms/search engines. It outlines serious incident reporting to the AI Office, cooperation among authorities, consultation before restrictive decisions, and AI Office responsibility for conformity assessments via notified bodies with fees paid by providers. It details procedures for market surveillance authorities requesting AI Office intervention. Article 75a defines the AI Office's supervisory and enforcement powers, cost recovery, investigation procedures, and information request mechanisms with associated fines for non-compliance.

nodes.title: Article 75a Supervisory and enforcement powers of the AI Office
nodes.summary: This text contains Articles 75a and 75b of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), detailing the supervisory and enforcement powers of the AI Office. Article 75a grants the AI Office market surveillance authority powers under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, including cost recovery from non-compliant operators. It can initiate investigations into suspected non-compliance by AI system providers or deployers, either independently or following complaints, and market surveillance authorities may refer matters to it. The AI Office can request information via simple request or decision, specifying legal basis, purpose, and applicable fines. It may conduct remote or on-site inspections, with powers to enter premises, examine records, make copies, question personnel, and seal premises, with national authority assistance and judicial authorization where required. Member State authorities may conduct investigations on its behalf. It may order access to AI systems, require data retention, appoint external experts, and must use collected information solely for this Regulation. Article 75b allows the AI Office to make operator commitments binding and specifies conditions for reopening or rejecting proceedings.

nodes.title: Article 75b Commitments
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (as amended) outlines enforcement powers of the AI Office. Article 75a(5-8) allows Member State market surveillance authorities to conduct investigations on behalf of the AI Office, grants the AI Office powers to order operator access/explanations and data retention, permits appointment of independent experts and auditors (with information shared with competent authorities), and restricts use of collected information to the Regulation's purposes. Article 75b addresses commitments: the AI Office may make operator commitments binding, reopen proceedings if facts change, commitments are breached, or information was misleading, and reject inadequate commitments. Article 75c covers non-compliance: the AI Office issues decisions establishing non-compliance after communicating preliminary findings, may order corrective measures within set periods, engage in structured dialogue, and impose administrative fines under Article 99(3)-(7) for infringements, non-compliance with decisions, breach of binding commitments, or supplying incorrect information. It may also impose periodic penalty payments to compel investigations or information submission.

nodes.title: Article 75c Non-compliance, fines and periodic penalty payments
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (Articles 75c and part of 75d) outlines the AI Office's enforcement powers regarding non-compliance. Article 75c establishes that upon finding non-compliance, the AI Office must communicate preliminary findings before adopting a decision ordering corrective measures, potentially after structured dialogue with the operator. Decisions may include administrative fines under Article 99(3)-(7) for infringements, failure to comply with decisions/measures, or breach of binding commitments; supplying incorrect information is also fineable. The AI Office may impose periodic penalty payments (up to 5% of average daily income/worldwide annual turnover) to compel compliance with investigations, information requests, inspections, corrective actions, commitments, or decisions. The Court of Justice has unlimited jurisdiction to review such penalties. Collected funds go to the EU budget. A five-year limitation period applies to enforcement powers. Proceedings may be closed if no non-compliance is found. Article 75d applies Article 18 of Regulation 2019/1020 mutatis mutandis as a safeguard.

nodes.title: Article 75d Safeguards and further specification
nodes.summary: This text from Regulation 2024/1689 (as amended) covers enforcement provisions by the AI Office. Article 75c lists grounds for penalty payments (failure to comply with inspections, provide correct answers, follow corrective actions, honor binding commitments, or comply with decisions), capped at 5% of daily income/annual turnover. It establishes Court of Justice jurisdiction to review fines, allocates collected funds to the EU budget, sets a five-year limitation period for enforcement, and allows closure of proceedings when no non-compliance exists. Article 75d addresses safeguards, applying Regulation 2019/1020 Article 18 mutatis mutandis, ensuring rights of defence and file access under negotiated disclosure (excluding confidential/internal documents), empowering the Commission to adopt implementing acts, and requiring publication of decisions respecting confidentiality. Article 76 governs market surveillance authorities' supervision of real-world testing, including references to Article 60a, verification within AI regulatory sandboxes, and authority to act on serious incidents or non-compliance.

nodes.title: Article 76 Supervision of testing in real world conditions by market surveillance authorities
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers procedural and supervisory rules. It outlines rights of defence and file access for operators under Article 75(1), including negotiated disclosure terms protecting business secrets, exclusions for confidential/internal documents, Commission implementing acts on access arrangements, and publication requirements for AI Office decisions. Article 76 addresses market surveillance authorities' supervision of real-world AI testing, including their competences, verification of compliance within regulatory sandboxes, powers to suspend/terminate/modify testing upon serious incidents or non-compliance, requirements to justify decisions and inform other Member States. Article 77 grants fundamental rights authorities powers to request accessible, machine-readable information from market surveillance authorities necessary for their mandates, obliges market surveillance authorities to provide such access promptly, mandates close cooperation and mutual assistance between authorities, and requires Member States to identify and publicly list these authorities by 2 November 2024, notifying the Commission and keeping lists updated.

nodes.title: Article 77 Powers of authorities protecting fundamental rights and cooperation with market surveillance authorities
nodes.summary: This excerpt from Regulation 2024/1689 covers provisions on real-world AI testing oversight and authority powers. Market surveillance authorities may suspend/terminate testing or require modifications, must justify such decisions, explain challenge procedures, and inform authorities in other Member States. Article 77 grants national public authorities protecting fundamental rights (including non-discrimination) powers to request accessible, machine-readable information from market surveillance authorities. These authorities must cooperate, exchange information, and provide mutual assistance. Member States must identify and publish lists of such bodies by 2 November 2024. Where documentation is insufficient, authorities may request technical testing of high-risk AI systems. Article 78 establishes confidentiality obligations for the Commission, market surveillance authorities, notified bodies, and others, protecting IP rights, trade secrets, source code, enforcement effectiveness, national security, legal proceedings, and classified information. Authorities must request only necessary data, implement cybersecurity measures, and delete data when no longer needed.

nodes.title: Article 78 Confidentiality
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 77-79. Article 77 (continued) allows public authorities to request market surveillance authorities to organize technical testing of high-risk AI systems when documentation is insufficient to assess fundamental rights infringements, with information handled per confidentiality rules. Article 78 establishes confidentiality obligations for the Commission, market surveillance authorities, notified bodies, and others, protecting IP rights, trade secrets, source code, enforcement effectiveness, security interests, proceedings, and classified information. It limits data requests to what is strictly necessary, mandates cybersecurity measures, and addresses special protections for law enforcement, border, immigration, and asylum uses of high-risk AI (Annex III points 1, 6, 7), including document access rules for cleared personnel. It permits confidential information exchange with third-country regulators under agreements. Article 79 defines AI systems presenting a risk per Regulation 2019/1020 and requires market surveillance authorities to evaluate compliance, prioritizing vulnerable groups and cooperating with fundamental rights authorities.

nodes.title: Article 79 Procedure at national level for dealing with AI systems presenting a risk
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers confidentiality and risk procedures. Article 78(3-5) addresses confidential information exchange: restrictions when high-risk AI systems in Annex III (points 1, 6, 7) are used by law enforcement, border, immigration or asylum authorities; keeping technical documentation on-premises with security-cleared access; preserving existing information-sharing obligations; and allowing confidential exchanges with third-country regulators under adequate arrangements. Article 79 establishes the national procedure for AI systems presenting risks: market surveillance authorities evaluate compliance, require corrective actions/withdrawal/recall (within 15 working days), inform the Commission and Member States, take provisional measures if operators fail to act, and notify details of non-compliance (including breaches of Article 5, Chapter III Section 2, Articles 40/41, or 50). Objections must be raised within three months (30 days for Article 5 breaches). Article 80 covers procedures when providers misclassify AI systems as non-high-risk under Article 6(3), requiring evaluation, corrective action, cross-border notification, and fines under Article 99 for non-compliance.

nodes.title: Article 80 Procedure for dealing with AI systems classified by the provider as non-high-risk in application of AnnexIII
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 79(7-9), 80, and 81 regarding market surveillance procedures for AI systems. Article 79 continues on notification duties between market surveillance authorities, the Commission, and Member States, deeming provisional measures justified if no objections arise within three months (30 days for prohibited AI practices under Article 5), and requiring restrictive measures like market withdrawal. Article 80 outlines procedures for AI systems misclassified by providers as non-high-risk under Annex III, requiring market surveillance authorities to evaluate, demand corrective action, inform the Commission and Member States, impose fines under Article 99 for non-compliance or deliberate circumvention, and conduct checks using the EU database. Article 81 establishes the Union safeguard procedure, enabling Commission consultation and evaluation when objections arise, decision timelines (six months or 60 days), binding effects on Member States, and application of Regulation 1025/2012 procedures when non-compliance stems from harmonised standards shortcomings.

nodes.title: Article 81 Union safeguard procedure
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers enforcement provisions. It outlines provider obligations to take corrective action across AI systems on the Union market, with fines applicable under Article 99 if a system was misclassified as non-high-risk to circumvent requirements. Market surveillance authorities may perform checks using the EU database. Article 81 establishes the Union safeguard procedure, allowing the Commission to evaluate contested national measures within six months (or 60 days for prohibited AI practices under Article 5), with binding consequences for Member States. Article 82 addresses compliant AI systems that still pose risks to health, safety, fundamental rights, or public interest, requiring corrective measures, Commission notification, and evaluation. Article 83 lists formal non-compliance findings requiring remediation, including improper or missing CE marking, missing or incorrect EU declaration of conformity, failure to register in the EU database, lack of an authorised representative, and unavailable technical documentation.

nodes.title: Article 82 Compliant AI systems which present a risk
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers two articles on AI system compliance. Article 82 addresses compliant high-risk AI systems that still present risks to health, safety, fundamental rights, or public interest. It requires market surveillance authorities to mandate corrective measures from operators, obliges providers to act on all affected AI systems in the Union market, requires Member States to inform the Commission and other Member States with relevant details (identification, origin, supply chain, risk nature, measures taken), and tasks the Commission with evaluating national measures, deciding on justification, proposing additional measures, and communicating decisions. Article 83 addresses formal non-compliance, requiring market surveillance authorities to demand providers end non-compliance in cases involving: improper or missing CE marking (Article 48), missing or incorrect EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), failure to register in the EU database (Article 71), lack of appointed authorised representative, or unavailable technical documentation.

nodes.title: Article 83 Formal non-compliance
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers Articles 82-86 on AI system compliance and remedies. Article 82 addresses compliant high-risk AI systems that still present risks, requiring operators to take corrective measures, with Member States informing the Commission, which evaluates and decides on justification. Article 83 covers formal non-compliance issues (CE marking violations, missing EU declaration of conformity, lack of EU database registration, no authorised representative, unavailable technical documentation), requiring providers to remedy them or face market restrictions. Article 84 establishes Union AI testing support structures designated by the Commission to perform tasks under Regulation 2019/1020 and provide technical/scientific advice. Article 85 grants natural/legal persons the right to lodge complaints with market surveillance authorities. Article 86 provides affected persons the right to obtain clear explanations from deployers about high-risk AI system decisions (per Annex III, excluding point 2) producing legal or significant effects, subject to exceptions under Union/national law.

nodes.title: Article 84 Union AI testing support structures
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers enforcement and remedies for AI systems. It states that when non-compliance persists, market surveillance authorities must take proportionate measures to restrict, prohibit, recall, or withdraw high-risk AI systems. Article 84 mandates the Commission to designate Union AI testing support structures to perform tasks under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and provide independent technical or scientific advice to the Board, Commission, or market surveillance authorities. Section 4 on Remedies includes Article 85, granting any natural or legal person the right to lodge complaints with market surveillance authorities regarding infringements. Article 86 provides affected persons the right to obtain clear, meaningful explanations from deployers about the role of high-risk AI systems (listed in Annex III, excluding point 2) in decisions producing legal or similarly significant adverse effects on health, safety, or fundamental rights, subject to exceptions under Union/national law and only where not otherwise provided.

This section (Articles 74-86) sets out the enforcement framework of the EU AI Act. It applies Regulation 2019/1020 to AI systems and designates market surveillance authorities for different categories (high-risk, financial, law enforcement, EU institutions), granting access to documentation, datasets, and source code with confidentiality safeguards. It establishes the AI Office's exclusive competence over AI systems built on general-purpose AI models and those integrated into very large online platforms, detailing its supervisory and investigatory powers, inspections, information requests, binding commitments, non-compliance decisions, administrative fines, periodic penalty payments (up to 5% of turnover), limitation periods, procedural safeguards, and rights of defence. It covers supervision of real-world testing, cooperation with fundamental rights authorities, confidentiality obligations, national and Union safeguard procedures, handling of risky or misclassified systems, formal non-compliance remedies, Union AI testing support structures, and remedies including the right to lodge complaints and obtain explanations of high-risk AI decisions.

nodes.title: SECTION 4 Remedies
key_items: Article 85 Right to lodge a complaint with a market surveillance authority
Article 86 Right to explanation of individual decision-making
Article 87 Reporting of infringements and protection of reporting persons
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers enforcement and remedies provisions. It mandates market surveillance authorities to restrict, recall, or withdraw non-compliant high-risk AI systems (Art. 83 continued). Article 84 establishes Union AI testing support structures designated by the Commission to provide technical/scientific advice. Section 4 on remedies grants rights to lodge complaints with market surveillance authorities (Art. 85), the right of affected persons to obtain clear explanations of decisions made via high-risk AI systems in Annex III (Art. 86, with exceptions), and applies Directive 2019/1937 to whistleblower protection (Art. 87). Section 5 addresses general-purpose AI model providers: Article 88 gives the Commission exclusive supervisory/enforcement powers via the AI Office; Article 89 empowers the AI Office to monitor compliance and allows downstream providers to file reasoned complaints specifying contact details, relevant facts/provisions, and supporting information.

nodes.title: SECTION 5 Supervision, investigation, enforcement and monitoring in respect of providers of general-purpose AI models
Article 88 Enforcement of the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), effective 27.07.2026, covers Article 87, which applies Directive (EU) 2019/1937 to the reporting of infringements and protection of whistleblowers. Section 5 addresses supervision, investigation, enforcement, and monitoring of general-purpose AI model providers. Article 88 grants the Commission exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, delegating implementation to the AI Office, while allowing market surveillance authorities to request Commission intervention when necessary. Article 89 empowers the AI Office to monitor compliance by general-purpose AI model providers, including adherence to codes of practice. It also grants downstream providers the right to file reasoned complaints alleging infringements, which must include: (a) the contact point of the concerned provider, (b) a description of relevant facts, applicable provisions, and reasoning for the alleged infringement, and (c) any other relevant information, including self-gathered data.

nodes.title: Article 89 Monitoring actions
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act), Articles 87-91, covers reporting and enforcement provisions. Article 87 applies Directive (EU) 2019/1937 to infringement reporting and whistleblower protection. Section 5 addresses supervision of general-purpose AI model providers: Article 88 grants the Commission exclusive enforcement powers over Chapter V, delegated to the AI Office, with market surveillance authorities able to request Commission intervention. Article 89 empowers the AI Office to monitor compliance, including code of practice adherence, and allows downstream providers to lodge reasoned complaints with specified content requirements. Article 90 permits the scientific panel to issue qualified alerts about identifiable Union-level risks or models meeting Article 51 conditions, triggering Commission assessment powers. Article 91 grants the Commission authority to request documentation/information from providers under Articles 53 and 55, allows structured dialogue via the AI Office, enables scientific panel-initiated requests, and requires requests to state legal basis, purpose, deadline, and applicable fines.

nodes.title: Article 90 Alerts of systemic risks by the scientific panel
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers Articles 90 and 91 regarding oversight of general-purpose AI models. Article 90 establishes that a scientific panel may issue qualified alerts to the AI Office when suspecting a general-purpose AI model poses identifiable Union-level risk or meets Article 51 conditions. Upon such alert, the Commission, via the AI Office and after informing the Board, may exercise assessment powers. Qualified alerts must be reasoned and include the provider's contact point, relevant facts and reasoning, and any other pertinent information. Article 91 grants the Commission power to request documentation and information from providers to assess compliance under Articles 53 and 55. The AI Office may initiate structured dialogue beforehand. Requests may also follow substantiated scientific panel requests when necessary and proportionate for tasks under Article 68(2). Requests must state legal basis, purpose, required information, response deadline, and fines under Article 101 for incorrect submissions.

nodes.title: Article 91 Power to request documentation and information
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 90-92 regarding oversight of general-purpose AI models. Article 90 allows the scientific panel to issue qualified alerts to the AI Office when suspecting a model poses Union-level risks or meets Article 51 conditions, specifying required alert contents (provider contact, facts, reasoning). Article 91 grants the Commission power to request documentation and information from providers, optionally preceded by structured dialogue, including requests triggered by the scientific panel; requests must state legal basis, purpose, deadline, and applicable fines under Article 101. Providers or authorized representatives/lawyers must supply information, with clients remaining responsible. Article 92 empowers the AI Office, after consulting the Board, to conduct evaluations to assess compliance or investigate systemic risks, potentially using independent experts, with access via APIs or source code. Implementing acts will detail evaluation procedures via the examination procedure in Article 98(2).

nodes.title: Article 92 Power to conduct evaluations
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers provisions on general-purpose AI models and codes of conduct. Article 91(5) specifies who must supply requested information on behalf of providers. Article 92 grants the AI Office power to conduct evaluations to assess compliance or investigate systemic risks, allowing appointment of independent experts, API/source code access requests, and provisions for structured dialogue with providers. Article 93 empowers the Commission to request providers to take compliance measures, implement risk mitigation, or restrict/withdraw/recall models, with provisions for binding commitments through structured dialogue. Article 94 extends procedural rights under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 to general-purpose AI model providers. Chapter X begins with Article 95, under which the AI Office and Member States encourage voluntary codes of conduct for non-high-risk AI systems to apply Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, considering technical solutions and industry best practices. Implementing acts follow the examination procedure in Article 98(2).

nodes.title: Commission Powers and Procedural Rights on General-Purpose AI Models
key_items: Article 94 Procedural rights of economic operators of the general-purpose AI model
nodes.summary: This page from Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 covers Commission oversight of general-purpose AI models. It notes the AI Office may initiate a structured dialogue with providers before requesting model access to gather information on internal testing, safeguards, and risk mitigation procedures. Article 93 empowers the Commission to request providers to comply with Articles 53 and 54 obligations, implement mitigation measures where systemic risks are identified under Article 92, or restrict, withdraw, or recall the model; a prior structured dialogue is possible, and provider commitments may be made binding by Commission decision. Article 94 applies Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 mutatis mutandis to providers, preserving more specific procedural rights. The page also begins Chapter X on Codes of Conduct, with Article 95 encouraging voluntary codes extending Chapter III, Section 2 requirements to non-high-risk AI systems based on available technical solutions and industry best practices.

Section 5 of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) establishes the supervision, investigation, enforcement, and monitoring framework for providers of general-purpose AI models. Article 88 grants the Commission exclusive enforcement powers over Chapter V obligations, delegated to the AI Office, with market surveillance authorities able to request Commission intervention. Article 89 empowers the AI Office to monitor compliance, including adherence to codes of practice, and allows downstream providers to lodge reasoned complaints with specified content (contact point, facts, reasoning, supporting information). Article 90 enables the scientific panel to issue qualified alerts about systemic or Union-level risks, triggering Commission assessment. Article 91 authorizes the Commission to request documentation and information from providers, optionally via structured dialogue, specifying legal basis, purpose, deadline, and fines, and designates who must supply information. Article 92 empowers the AI Office to conduct evaluations using independent experts, with API/source code access. Article 93 allows the Commission to require compliance measures, risk mitigation, or model restriction/withdrawal/recall, with binding commitments possible. Article 94 extends procedural rights under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 to providers.

Chapter IX of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) governs post-market monitoring, information sharing, and market surveillance. Section 1 establishes the EU database for high-risk AI systems, data-entry duties, accessibility, and requires providers to implement proportionate post-market monitoring systems and plans (Commission template by September 2027). Section 2 details serious-incident reporting timelines (15 days generally, 2 days for widespread infringements, 10 days for deaths), investigation duties, and sector-specific rules. Section 3 (Articles 74–86) sets the enforcement framework, applying Regulation 2019/1020, designating market surveillance authorities, granting AI Office exclusive competence over general-purpose AI systems, with powers of inspection, information requests, fines up to 5% turnover, penalty payments, safeguards, and cooperation with fundamental rights bodies. Section 4 provides remedies: complaints, explanations of high-risk AI decisions, whistleblower protection. Section 5 regulates general-purpose AI model providers via Commission/AI Office supervision, downstream complaints, scientific-panel alerts, information requests, evaluations, compliance measures, and procedural rights.

nodes.title: CHAPTER X CODES OF CONDUCT AND GUIDELINES
key_items: Article 95 Codes of conduct for voluntary application of specific requirements
Article 96 Guidelines from the Commission on the implementation of this Regulation
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers Articles 93-97. Article 93 empowers the Commission to request providers of general-purpose AI models to take compliance measures, implement risk mitigation, or restrict/withdraw/recall models, with provisions for structured dialogue and binding commitments. Article 94 extends procedural rights under Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 to such providers. Chapter X addresses codes of conduct: Article 95 encourages voluntary codes for non-high-risk AI systems, covering ethical guidelines, environmental sustainability, AI literacy, inclusive design, and protection of vulnerable groups, with attention to SMEs. Article 96 mandates Commission guidelines on practical implementation covering requirements, prohibited practices, substantial modifications, transparency, relationship with Union harmonisation law, AI system definition, and complementarity principles, involving the Board and considering SMEs. Chapter XI begins with Article 97 on delegation of power, specifying five-year delegation periods from August 2024 or July 2026 for various articles, with tacit extension provisions.

nodes.title: CHAPTER XI DELEGATION OF POWER AND COMMITTEE PROCEDURE
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers several provisions. Article 96 outlines Commission guidelines on practical implementation of transparency obligations, relationship with Union harmonisation legislation, definition of AI systems, and application of specific articles (to be published by August 2027), involving the Board and considering SMEs, start-ups, SMCs, local authorities, and relevant harmonised standards. Guidelines may be updated as needed. Chapter XI addresses delegation of power: Article 97 confers delegated act powers on the Commission for five-year renewable periods (from August 2024 or July 2026 for specific articles), with revocation rights by Parliament or Council, consultation requirements, notification procedures, and a three-month objection period. Article 98 establishes committee procedure under Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. Chapter XII begins with Article 99 on penalties, requiring Member States to establish effective, proportionate, dissuasive penalties (including administrative fines, warnings, non-monetary measures) while considering SME and SMC economic viability.

nodes.title: CHAPTER XII PENALTIES
Article 99 Penalties
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 covers provisions on delegated acts, committee procedure, and penalties. It details how the European Parliament or Council can revoke delegated powers, the Commission's obligation to consult Member State experts, notification requirements, and the three-month objection period for delegated acts (Article 97 context). Article 98 establishes committee assistance under Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. Chapter XII on Penalties (Article 99) requires Member States to set effective, proportionate, dissuasive penalties, considering SMEs/start-ups/SMCs. It specifies fines: up to €35M or 7% turnover for Article 5 violations; €15M or 3% for other operator/notified body obligations; €7.5M or 1% for providing incorrect information. Lower caps apply to SMEs and SMCs. It lists factors for determining fines (nature, gravity, cooperation, intent, etc.), rules for public authorities, procedural safeguards, and annual reporting. Article 100 empowers the European Data Protection Supervisor to fine Union institutions, with up to €1.5M for Article 5 violations.

nodes.title: Article 100 Administrative fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers administrative fines provisions. Article 99 (concluding paragraphs) requires procedural safeguards and annual Member State reporting to the Commission on fines and litigation. Article 100 empowers the European Data Protection Supervisor to impose fines on Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, listing factors to consider (nature/gravity of infringement, responsibility, mitigation, cooperation, prior infringements, notification manner, annual budget). It sets fine caps: up to EUR 1,500,000 for violations of Article 5 prohibitions and EUR 750,000 for other non-compliance. It mandates the right to be heard, defence rights, file access, allocation of fines to the Union budget, and annual Commission notification. Article 101 allows the Commission to fine providers of general-purpose AI models up to 3% of worldwide turnover or EUR 15,000,000 for intentional/negligent infringements, non-compliance with information requests (Article 91), measures (Article 93), or evaluation access (Article 92).

nodes.title: Article 101 Fines for providers of general-purpose AI models
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers administrative fines and final provisions. It specifies fines up to EUR 750,000 for AI system non-compliance by Union institutions outside Article 5. It details European Data Protection Supervisor procedures, including the right to be heard, rights of defense, file access, allocation of fine proceeds to the Union budget, and annual reporting to the Commission. Article 101 establishes fines for general-purpose AI model providers up to 3% of worldwide turnover or EUR 15 million for intentional/negligent infringements, non-compliance with information requests, Article 93 measures, or model access for evaluation. It outlines proportionality considerations, preliminary findings communication, Court of Justice unlimited review jurisdiction, Board notification, and implementing acts for procedural safeguards. Chapter XIII begins with final provisions: Article 102 amends Regulation (EC) No 300/2008 regarding AI security equipment requirements, and Article 103 begins amending Regulation (EU) No 167/2013.

Chapter XII of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) establishes penalties for AI-related infringements. Article 99 requires Member States to set effective, proportionate, dissuasive penalties, considering SMEs, start-ups, and SMCs. It sets fines up to €35M or 7% of turnover for Article 5 prohibition violations; €15M or 3% for other operator and notified body obligations; and €7.5M or 1% for providing incorrect information, with lower caps for SMEs. It lists factors for determining fines (nature, gravity, intent, cooperation), rules for public authorities, procedural safeguards, and annual reporting to the Commission. Article 100 empowers the European Data Protection Supervisor to fine Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies—up to €1.5M for Article 5 violations and €750,000 otherwise—with defence rights, file access, and budget allocation. Article 101 allows the Commission to fine general-purpose AI model providers up to 3% of worldwide turnover or €15M, subject to Court of Justice review.

nodes.title: CHAPTER XIII FINAL PROVISIONS
Article 102 Amendment to Regulation(EC) No300/2008
nodes.summary: This excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers rules on fines and periodic penalty payments for providers of general-purpose AI models. It specifies that fines must consider the nature, gravity, and duration of infringements, proportionality, and commitments under Article 93(3) or codes of practice. The Commission must communicate preliminary findings and allow the provider to be heard before deciding. Fines must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive, with information shared with the Board. The Court of Justice of the EU has unlimited jurisdiction to review, cancel, reduce, or increase fines. The Commission will adopt implementing acts detailing procedural safeguards via examination procedure under Article 98(2). Chapter XIII (Final Provisions) begins with Article 102, amending Regulation (EC) No 300/2008 to require consideration of Chapter III, Section 2 requirements when adopting measures on AI-related security equipment, and Article 103 introduces an amendment to Regulation (EU) No 167/2013.

nodes.title: Article 103 Amendment to Regulation(EU) No167/2013
nodes.summary: This excerpt from Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers rules on fines for general-purpose AI model providers and amendments to related regulations. It specifies that fines must consider the infringement's nature, gravity, duration, proportionality, and compliance commitments. The Commission must communicate preliminary findings and allow a hearing before issuing decisions. Fines must be effective, proportionate, dissuasive, and reported to the Board. The Court of Justice has unlimited jurisdiction to review, cancel, reduce, or increase fines. The Commission will adopt implementing acts detailing procedural safeguards. Chapter XIII final provisions include Articles 102–105, amending Regulation (EC) No 300/2008 (aviation security), Regulation (EU) No 167/2013 (agricultural vehicles), Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 (two/three-wheel vehicles), and Directive 2014/90/EU (marine equipment), requiring that when adopting measures or delegated acts concerning AI systems that are safety components, the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 of the AI Act must be considered.

nodes.title: Article 104 Amendment to Regulation(EU) No168/2013
nodes.summary: This text chunk from Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), dated 27.07.2026, contains three articles amending existing EU legislation to incorporate AI-related requirements. Article 103 (implied continuation) and Article 104 amend Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 (Article 22(5)), adding a subparagraph requiring that when adopting delegated acts concerning AI systems that are safety components, the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 of the AI Act must be taken into account. Article 105 amends Directive 2014/90/EU by adding paragraph 5 to Article 8, requiring the Commission to consider the same AI Act requirements when carrying out activities and adopting technical specifications and testing standards for AI systems serving as safety components. Each amendment includes a footnote citing the full title and publication reference of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), published in OJ L on 12.7.2024.

nodes.title: Article 105 Amendment to Directive 2014/90/EU
nodes.summary: This text contains Articles 104-108 of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (the Artificial Intelligence Act), which introduce consistent amendments to several existing EU legal instruments concerning sectoral product safety. Specifically, it amends Regulation (EU) No 168/2013 (Article 104), Directive 2014/90/EU on marine equipment (Article 105), Directive (EU) 2016/797 on rail interoperability (Article 106), Regulation (EU) 2018/858 on motor vehicle approval (Article 107), and Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 on civil aviation (Article 108). Each amendment adds a new paragraph requiring that, when adopting delegated or implementing acts concerning AI systems that function as safety components under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 of the AI Act must be taken into account. Each amendment includes an identical footnote citing the full title and publication reference of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

nodes.title: Amendments to Sectoral EU Legislation for AI Safety Components
nodes.summary: This page from Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act) contains amendments to existing EU sectoral legislation to ensure AI safety component requirements are considered. Article 106 amends Directive (EU) 2016/797 (rail interoperability) by adding paragraph 12 to Article 5, requiring that when adopting delegated and implementing acts concerning AI systems that are safety components, the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 of the AI Act must be taken into account. Article 107 amends Regulation (EU) 2018/858 (motor vehicle approval) by adding paragraph 4 to Article 5 with the same obligation for delegated acts. The page also begins Article 108, amending Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (civil aviation) by adding paragraph 3 to Article 17, imposing the same requirement for implementing acts. Each amendment includes a footnote citing the AI Act's full title and publication reference.

nodes.title: Article 108 Amendments to Regulation(EU) 2018/1139
nodes.summary: This text contains Articles 106-109 of the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), which introduce amendments to several existing EU legal instruments. Article 106 amends Directive (EU) 2016/797 (rail interoperability), Article 107 amends Regulation (EU) 2018/858 (motor vehicle approval), Article 108 amends Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 (civil aviation) across six provisions (Articles 17, 19, 43, 47, 57, and 58), and Article 109 amends Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 (vehicle safety). Each amendment adds a new paragraph requiring that, when adopting delegated or implementing acts concerning AI systems that qualify as safety components under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2 of that Regulation must be taken into account. Each amendment also includes a footnote citing the full title and publication reference of the AI Act.

nodes.title: Article 109 Amendment to Regulation(EU) 2019/2144
nodes.summary: This text contains amendments to EU regulations and transitional provisions under the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689). It adds paragraphs to Articles 19, 43, 47, 57, and 58 of an existing regulation, requiring that when adopting delegated or implementing acts concerning AI systems that are safety components, the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 of Regulation 2024/1689 must be considered. Article 109 similarly amends Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/2144, and Article 110 adds the AI Act to Annex I of Directive (EU) 2020/1828. Article 111 sets transitional rules: AI systems in large-scale IT systems placed on market before 2 August 2027 must comply by 31 December 2030; high-risk AI systems with significant design changes must comply, with public authority systems complying by 2 August 2030; general-purpose AI model providers must comply by 2 August 2027; and synthetic content generators must comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026.

nodes.title: Article 110 Amendment to Directive(EU) 2020/1828
nodes.summary: This excerpt from the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) covers Articles 110 and 111. Article 110 amends Directive (EU) 2020/1828 by adding the AI Act to its Annex I list of regulations covered for representative consumer actions. Article 111 sets transitional provisions for AI systems and models already on the market: (1) AI components of large-scale IT systems listed in Annex X placed on the market before 2 August 2027 must comply by 31 December 2030; (2) the Regulation applies to high-risk AI systems placed on the market before Chapter III's application date only if significantly redesigned afterward, while providers/deployers serving public authorities must comply by 2 August 2030; (3) providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply by 2 August 2027; (4) providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text content placed on the market before 2 August 2026 must comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026.

nodes.title: Article 111 AI systems already placed on the market or put into service and general-purpose AI models already placed on the marked
nodes.summary: This excerpt from the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) covers Articles 110-112. Article 110 amends Directive (EU) 2020/1828 by adding the AI Act to Annex I. Article 111 sets transition deadlines for existing AI systems: large-scale IT systems (Annex X) must comply by 31 December 2030; high-risk AI systems placed on the market before Chapter III's application date must comply only if significantly redesigned, with public authority systems required to comply by 2 August 2030; general-purpose AI model providers must comply by 2 August 2027; and providers of AI generating synthetic content must comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026. Article 112 establishes evaluation and review obligations: annual Commission assessments of Annex III and Article 5 lists; quadrennial reports starting 2 August 2028 on amendments, transparency, and governance; review reports from 2 August 2029; focus on resources, penalties, standards, and SMEs; and an AI Office evaluation by 2 August 2028.

nodes.title: Article 112 Evaluation and review
key_items: 4. The reports referred to in paragraph 2 shall pay specific attention to the following:
nodes.summary: This text contains Articles 112 and 113 of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act). Article 112 covers evaluation and review obligations: the Commission must annually assess amendments to Annex III and prohibited AI practices (Article 5); evaluate every four years (from 2 August 2028) the need to amend area headings, transparency measures (Article 50), and governance; submit review reports every four years (from 2 August 2029) potentially proposing a Union agency; focus on national authorities' resources, penalties, harmonised standards, and SME market entry; evaluate the AI Office's powers by 2 August 2028; review energy-efficient general-purpose AI model standards; assess voluntary codes of conduct every three years; require cooperation from the Board and Member States; develop a participative risk-evaluation methodology; and conduct an enforcement assessment by 2 August 2031. Article 113 sets entry into force on the twentieth day post-publication, with general application from 2 August 2026 and staggered application dates for specific chapters/articles.

nodes.title: Article 113 Entry into force and application
nodes.summary: This text excerpt from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act) covers two main parts. First, Article 113 provisions include: a Commission assessment of enforcement by 2 August 2031 to be reported to the European Parliament, Council, and European Economic and Social Committee, potentially with amendment proposals regarding enforcement structure and the need for a Union agency. It also specifies entry into force (twentieth day after publication) and staggered application dates: general application from 2 August 2026, with Chapters I-II from 2 February 2025 (with exceptions until 2 December 2026), certain chapters from 2 August 2025, high-risk AI provisions from 2 December 2027 or 2 August 2028 depending on classification, and Articles 102-110 from 27 July 2026. Second, Annex I lists Union harmonisation legislation, including Section A (New Legislative Framework: toys, recreational craft, lifts, explosive atmospheres, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableways, PPE, gas appliances, medical devices) and Section B (civil aviation security).

Chapter XIII (Final Provisions) of the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) contains Articles 102–113. Articles 102–109 amend existing EU sectoral legislation—Regulation (EC) No 300/2008 (aviation security), Regulations (EU) No 167/2013 and 168/2013 (agricultural and two/three-wheel vehicles), Directive 2014/90/EU (marine equipment), Directive (EU) 2016/797 (rail interoperability), Regulations (EU) 2018/858 (motor vehicles), 2018/1139 (civil aviation), and 2019/2144 (vehicle safety)—requiring Chapter III, Section 2 AI Act requirements to be considered when adopting delegated or implementing acts on AI safety components. Article 110 adds the AI Act to Annex I of Directive (EU) 2020/1828 for representative consumer actions. Article 111 sets transitional compliance deadlines for pre-existing large-scale IT systems, high-risk AI systems, general-purpose AI models, and synthetic content generators. Article 112 establishes Commission evaluation, review, and reporting obligations. Article 113 defines entry into force and staggered application dates.

nodes.title: ANNEX I  List of Union harmonisation legislation
nodes.summary: This text contains two annexes from EU Regulation 2024/1689. Annex I lists Union harmonisation legislation in two sections: Section A covers legislation based on the New Legislative Framework, including directives and regulations on toy safety, recreational craft, lifts, equipment for explosive atmospheres, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableway installations, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, medical devices, and in vitro diagnostic medical devices. Section B lists other harmonisation legislation covering civil aviation security, two/three-wheel vehicles, agricultural/forestry vehicles, marine equipment, rail system interoperability, motor vehicle approval and safety, civil aviation (unmanned aircraft), and machinery. Annex II lists criminal offences referenced in Article 5(1)(h)(iii), including terrorism, human trafficking, child sexual exploitation, illicit drug/weapons/organ/nuclear material trafficking, murder, grievous bodily injury, kidnapping, International Criminal Court crimes, aircraft/ship seizure, rape, environmental crime, organised robbery, sabotage, and participation in related criminal organisations.

nodes.title: ANNEX II  List of criminal offences referred to in Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point(h)(iii)
nodes.summary: This text from EU Regulation 2024/1689 contains two annexes. Annex II lists criminal offences referenced in Article 5(1)(h)(iii), including terrorism, human trafficking, sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, illicit trafficking in drugs, weapons, human organs, or nuclear materials, murder, grievous bodily injury, kidnapping, hostage-taking, crimes under International Criminal Court jurisdiction, unlawful seizure of aircraft/ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in criminal organisations involved in these offences. Annex III lists high-risk AI systems under Article 6(2) across areas: (1) Biometrics (remote identification, categorisation by sensitive attributes, emotion recognition, excluding verification); (2) Critical infrastructure safety components (digital infrastructure, traffic, utilities); (3) Education and vocational training (admissions, learning evaluation, education level assessment, test monitoring); (4) Employment (recruitment, selection, work-relationship decisions, performance monitoring); and begins (5) Access to essential private and public services and benefits.

nodes.title: ANNEX III  High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
key_items: High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2)
nodes.summary: This text contains two annexes from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act). Annex III lists high-risk AI systems under Article 6(2) across eight areas: (1) Biometrics (remote identification, categorisation by sensitive attributes, emotion recognition); (2) Critical infrastructure safety components; (3) Education and vocational training (admissions, learning evaluation, test monitoring); (4) Employment (recruitment, performance evaluation, task allocation); (5) Essential private and public services (benefits eligibility, creditworthiness, insurance risk assessment, emergency call triage); (6) Law enforcement (victim/offender risk assessment, polygraphs, evidence reliability, profiling); (7) Migration, asylum and border control (polygraphs, risk assessment, application examination, identification); (8) Administration of justice and democratic processes (judicial assistance, election influence). Annex IV specifies technical documentation requirements under Article 11(1), including a general AI system description (purpose, interactions, versions, hardware, user interface, instructions) and detailed descriptions of development elements (methods, design specifications, system architecture, computational resources).

nodes.title: ANNEX IV  Technical documentation referred to in Article 11(1)
key_items: Technical documentation referred to in Article 11(1)
nodes.summary: This text contains two annexes from EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act). Annex IV specifies the technical documentation required under Article 11(1) for AI systems, including: (1) general description (purpose, provider, versions, interactions, hardware, user interface, instructions); (2) detailed development elements (methods, design specifications, system architecture, data requirements, human oversight assessment, pre-determined changes, validation/testing procedures, cybersecurity); (3) monitoring, functioning and control information (capabilities, limitations, risks, oversight); (4) performance metrics appropriateness; (5) risk management system description; (6) lifecycle changes; (7) harmonised standards applied; (8) EU declaration of conformity copy; (9) post-market monitoring system. Annex V outlines the required contents of the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47: AI system identification, provider details, responsibility statement, conformity statements with the Regulation and data protection laws (GDPR, etc.), references to harmonised standards, notified body information where applicable, and signature details including place, date, and signatory.

nodes.title: ANNEX V  EU declaration of conformity
nodes.summary: This text contains two annexes from EU Regulation 2024/1689. Annex V specifies the required content of the EU declaration of conformity referenced in Article 47, including: AI system name/type and identification details; provider or authorised representative's name and address; statement that the declaration is issued under the provider's sole responsibility; statement of conformity with the Regulation and other relevant EU law; compliance statement with GDPR Regulations (EU) 2016/679, 2018/1725, and Directive 2016/680 when personal data is processed; references to harmonised standards or common specifications used; notified body details, conformity assessment procedure, and certificate information where applicable; and place, date, signatory details, and signature. Annex VI describes the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control, requiring the provider to verify the quality management system complies with Article 17, examine technical documentation for compliance with Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and ensure design, development, and post-market monitoring (Article 72) align with the technical documentation.

nodes.title: ANNEX VI  Conformity assessment procedure based on internal control
key_items: Conformity assessment procedure based on internal control
nodes.summary: This text contains Annexes VI and VII of EU Regulation 2024/1689 (AI Act).
